### I.6.6(c) is closed on Milne; the converse half of I.6.7 has no complete published solution

**Object and need.** Two requests in `SRC-TEXT-HART77` §I.6 are proved on their cards without a published argument to check against: `P-AGH66AUTP1` (I.6.6(c), printed p. 46), that every $k$-automorphism of $k(x)$ is a fractional linear transformation, and `P-AGH67PUNCTUREDLINE` (I.6.7, printed p. 47), the question "Is the converse true?" following $r=s$.

**Observed evidence.** Richard E. Borcherds, *Hartshorne, Chapter 1: Answers to exercises* (1994), Chapter 1.6, PDF p. 8, argues 6.6(c) by "if $f$ or $g$ have degree greater than 1 then $g(y)a=f(y)$ will usually have more than one solution for $y$", which is not an argument and misstates the equation ($f$ and $g$ are the coprime numerator and denominator of the image of $x$, so the equation to solve is $f(y)=a\,g(y)$); Andrew Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (October 3, 2013), PDF p. 55, writes "injectivity of $\phi$ $\Rightarrow$ $f,g$ are linear", and Joe Cutrone and Nick Marshburn, *Algebraic Geometry by Robin Hartshorne: Solutions*, PDF p. 25, write "if $\deg g,\deg f>1$, the map won't be injective". The inference is the content of the request and no set proves it. On 6.7 the same three sets answer $r=s$ and then give the threshold for the converse as $r\le3$ (Borcherds: "the converse is true if and only if $r\le3$"; Egbert: "the converse is only true for $r\le3$"; Cutrone--Marshburn: "the converse is not true for $r>3$"). That threshold is one too high: the extension of an isomorphism $\AA^1\setminus P\to\AA^1\setminus Q$ to an automorphism of $\PP^1$ carries the $(r+1)$-point set $\{\infty\}\cup P$ onto $\{\infty\}\cup Q$ --- the image of $\infty$ is whichever point of that set it is, and need not be $\infty$ --- and for $r=3$ the cross ratio of these four-point sets obstructs the converse, so the threshold is $r\le2$. Cutrone--Marshburn add that "any isomorphism between $\PP^1$ and $\PP^1$ fixes at most 2 points, so if $r>3$, the map must be the identity isomorphism"; the premise is true of a non-identity automorphism, but the inference is not, since an isomorphism carrying one of the two $(r+1)$-point sets to the other need not fix any of its points.

**Impact and owner.** Both cards keep complete proofs. 6.6(c) is Milne's argument transcribed since 2026-11-16 --- steps `degree-of-a-rational-function` (Lemma 9.24, printed p. 118) and `field-automorphism-fractional-linear` (Example 9.25, printed p. 119), text version `tmp/sources/milne-fields-and-galois-theory.md` --- and the card's earlier route, an automorphism fixing $\infty$ reduced to a $k$-algebra automorphism of $k[x]$ and $\deg x=\deg(q\circ p)$, was removed at `5ff1108be9` and is recorded only as the card's earlier one. 6.7's converse is settled by the four-point sets $\{\infty,0,1,\lambda\}$ and $\{\infty,0,1,\mu\}$ with $\mu$ outside the six cross-ratio transforms of $\lambda$, which exist because $k$ is infinite; step `converse-fails` now proves the invariance of the cross ratio and its six-value orbit from the one fact it needs, that an element of $\PGL(1)$ fixing $\infty$, $0$ and $1$ is the identity. What is missing is a published argument for the converse of 6.7.

**Uncertainty.** Searched: all twelve retained Hartshorne solution files in `tmp/sources` by `pdftotext -layout` extraction — Borcherds, Cais, Cutrone--Marshburn, Egbert, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Park, Saglam--Chris, Sam, Stein, Troiani — and the repository copy `assets/attachments/Hartshorne_Solutions.pdf`, whose provenance file records it as a byte-identical duplicate of the Cais notes. Found: Chapter I §6 material only in Borcherds (PDF p. 8), Egbert (PDF pp. 52--55) and Cutrone--Marshburn (PDF pp. 23--25). Troiani's Chapter I stops at §5 (PDF p. 16); Park's stops at §1; Sam's text layer is mirrored and was reversed line by line before searching, and its Chapter I ends at §4; Cais, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Saglam--Chris and Stein begin at Chapter II. Conclusion: no complete published solution for 6.6(c), and no correct published counterexample for the converse of 6.7. Confidence: high for these sets. Gaps: a published treatment may exist outside them.

**Repair.** A published proof of each, checked against the card, or the owner's direction to accept the cards' own derivations.

**Searched outside the retained sets (issue #131, 2026-11-11).** I.6.6(c) is closed: J. S. Milne, *Fields and Galois Theory*, Example 3.1(b) on printed p. 35 with Lemma 9.24 on printed p. 119, proves $[F(X):F(a_i)]=\deg(a_i)$ for $a_i$ in lowest terms and concludes that the $\CC$-automorphisms of $\CC(X)$ are exactly the fractional linear transformations; the same computation gives the step over any field. For the converse of I.6.7 nothing was located: the three retained sets all give the threshold $r\le3$, and a search of the same question outside them returned only those sets. The card's cross-ratio obstruction at $r=3$ is the counterexample they lack.

**Closed for I.6.6(c), 2026-11-16.** The card's proof of (c) is now Milne's argument transcribed, not merely cited: step `degree-of-a-rational-function` is Lemma 9.24 and step `field-automorphism-fractional-linear` is Example 9.25, which states $F(X)=F(u)$ if and only if $u=(aX+b)/(cX+d)$ with $ad-bc\ne0$ for an arbitrary field $F$. The page given for Lemma 9.24 in the paragraph above is wrong: the lemma, with its proof, is on printed p. 118 of the notes, text version `tmp/sources/milne-fields-and-galois-theory.md` beside the PDF `tmp/sources/milne-fields-and-galois-theory.pdf`, and Example 9.25 is on printed p. 119; both were re-read at those folios, and Example 3.1(b) on printed p. 35 is the $\CC$ case of the same conclusion. Checked against the book: Exercise I.6.6 on printed p. 46 asks (c) with Chapter I's $k$, which is fixed algebraically closed (text version `tmp/sources/hartshorne-1977-algebraic-geometry.md`, line 350), and part (b) appeals to Corollary I.6.12 in that setting; the exercise does not ask (c) over an arbitrary field, as this paragraph said until 2026-11-16. Milne's two results are stated over an arbitrary field, so the argument for (c) adds no hypothesis, and it is the proof the card carries. The converse half of I.6.7 stays open below.

**Searched again for the converse of I.6.7, 2026-11-16.** The Math Stack Exchange API (`search/advanced`, site `math`) was queried for "affine line minus n points isomorphic", "punctured affine line", "isomorphism punctured" and the exercise number; no thread on the converse of I.6.7, and no thread proving that $\AA^1$ minus three distinct points is not isomorphic to $\AA^1$ minus a generic other triple, was returned. A web search for the exercise with "cross ratio" returned the three retained sets, whose statements are quoted above, Wikipedia's cross-ratio article, which asserts that the cross ratio is the only projective invariant of an ordered quadruple without proof, and this repository's own pages. Nothing located gives a complete published counterexample; the card's step `converse-fails` is the counterexample the sources lack, and the check against the book is that Hartshorne's printed question on p. 47 is "Is the converse true?", so a counterexample and not a threshold is what answers it. The three sets' $r\le3$ is wrong for the reason recorded: the automorphism of $\PP^1$ carries the $(r+1)$-point set $\{\infty\}\cup P$ onto $\{\infty\}\cup Q$, so for $r=3$ the four-point cross ratio already obstructs it.

The nearest published text is Vakil, *The Rising Sea* (21 October 2025), §19.9.7 and Exercise 19.9.B, printed p. 557 (text version `tmp/sources/vakil-rising-sea-2025-10-21.md`): there $\Aut\PP^1$ is recorded as 3-transitive (his Exercise 15.5.B), the cross-ratio of four points is defined as the value $\lambda$ to which the fourth is carried once the other three go to $\infty,0,1$, and "isomorphism classes of four ordered distinct (closed) points on $\PP^1$ ... up to projective equivalence (automorphisms of $\PP^1$), are classified by the cross-ratio" is **Exercise 19.9.B**, that is, left to the reader. So the two inputs the card's obstruction uses are in print, one as an exercise and one as a cited exercise, and the counterexample itself is nowhere stated. That is the same obstacle as everywhere else in this entry: no complete published argument, and nothing that could be transcribed. Of the three facts step `converse-fails` uses, the uniqueness of the normalizing automorphism is printed in 19.9.7 (line 13770) and the six values in (19.9.7.1) (line 13797); the third, that an element of $\PGL(1)$ fixing $\infty$, $0$ and $1$ is the identity, is now proved on the card.
**2026-11-16: the converse of I.6.7 is assembled from printed statements.** `P-AGH67PUNCTUREDLINE`'s step `converse-fails` now names, at each paragraph, the printed fact it uses: Anders Kock, *Abstract Projective Lines* (4 December 2009), Theorem 1 on printed p. 6 (a projectivity is determined by the images of three distinct points, with existence), the paragraph after (8) on printed p. 5 (projectivities preserve cross ratios), the permutation laws (4)--(7) on printed p. 4 (the six values $\mu$, $1/\mu$, $1-\mu$, $1/(1-\mu)$, $\mu/(\mu-1)$ and $(\mu-1)/\mu$), and Section 4 on printed pp. 8--11 (the identification of $\PP^1$ with an abstract projective line, the determinant formula for the cross ratio, and the fractional linear form of a projectivity); with the accepted answer 834758 to question 834693 computing the same six values from the transpositions $(12)$, $(13)$, $(14)$ that generate $S_4$. Text versions `tmp/sources/kock-2009-abstract-projective-lines.md` and `tmp/sources/mse-834693-six-cross-ratio-values.md`. The part that is still open is the counterexample itself: no located source states that $\AA^1$ minus three points is not isomorphic to $\AA^1$ minus a generic other three, and the retained sets state a threshold instead, three of them a threshold one too high. What the card does is take the printed ingredients at $r=3$, where the four-point sets $\{\infty,0,1,\lambda\}$ and $\{\infty,0,1,\mu\}$ with $\mu$ outside the six values are separated by the cross ratio, and that one step --- that cross-ratio equivalence of the two ordered quadruples is what a fractional linear transformation carrying one set to the other amounts to --- is the card's. $r=s$ is Shichijo's, Chapter 1 section 6, Exercise 6.7, printed pp. 5--6, whose extension of the birational map to an automorphism of $\PP^1$ is transcribed on the card with the point $\infty$ written into his displayed exchange of the omitted sets.

**Correction, 2026-11-16, on the reader's report of #121: the I.6.7 entry restored.** The record above is one of the four restored in the I.3.16 entry, for the reason given there, and its corrections are these two. It gives the card's two four-point sets as $\{\infty,0,1,\lambda\}$ and $\{\infty,0,1,\mu\}$, which share $0$ and $1$ and so fail the exercise's hypothesis that all the $P_i$ and $Q_j$ be distinct; the card now takes $P=\{0,1,\lambda\}$ and $Q_\mu=\{a,b,\mu\}$ with $\lambda,a,b,\mu$ pairwise distinct, and reaches the cross-ratio condition through $\tau(x)=(x-a)/(b-a)$. And it places Kock's sentence that projectivities preserve cross ratios in "the paragraph after (8) on printed p. 5"; that sentence stands before display (8), which is where the card and its 2026-11-16 events place it.


### I.7.7(b) and the quadric half of I.7.8 have no complete published solution

**Object and need.** Two requests in `SRC-TEXT-HART77` §I.7 are proved on their cards without a published argument to check against: `P-AGH77CONEDEGDROP` (I.7.7(b), printed p. 55), that the join $X$ of a nonsingular point $P$ with a variety $Y^r$ of degree $d>1$ has $\deg X<d$; and `P-AGH78DEGTWOSPAN` (I.7.8, printed p. 55), that a variety $Y^r\subseteq\PP^n$ of degree $2$ sits in a linear subspace of dimension $r+1$ **and** is a quadric hypersurface there.

**Observed evidence.** For I.7.7(b) all three sets that reach the section take the printed induction on $\dim Y$. Andrew Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (October 3, 2013), Exercise I.7.7, PDF p. 58, writes "by Thm 7.7, 7.6b, $\deg X\cap H=\deg X$. By induction $\deg X\cap H\le\deg Y\cap H\le\deg Y=d$"; Joe Cutrone and Nick Marshburn, *Algebraic Geometry by Robin Hartshorne: Solutions*, PDF p. 27, writes "choose a hyperplane $H$ through $P$ not containing $Y$ so that the intersection multiplicity along any component of $X\cap H$ is $1$. Then by Thm 7.7 and 7.6(b), $\deg X\cap H=\deg X$". Both identities are steps of the induction and neither is proved. Richard E. Borcherds, *Hartshorne, Chapter 1: Answers to exercises* (1994), Exercise 7.7, PDF pp. 9--10, states the genericity the argument needs — a generic hyperplane through $P$ meeting $Y$ and $X$ transversely, and $X\cap H$ irreducible — and refers the second of these to remark III.7.9.1 with Bertini (II, 8.18), which is quoted rather than applied; his induction also has to know that $X\cap H$ is the cone on $Y\cap H$, which holds only when the section is the join of the same vertex with $Y\cap H$. For I.7.8 all three prove the linear span and stop: Borcherds "applying 7.7 to $Y^r$ shows that $Y$ is contained in a degree $1$ variety $H$ of dimension $r+1$ in $\PP^n$, which by 7.6 is a linear variety and therefore isomorphic to $\PP^{r+1}$"; Egbert and Cutrone--Marshburn the same with the two exercise references. The second sentence of the printed exercise, that $Y$ is a quadric hypersurface in that span, is asserted by all three and proved by none.

**Impact and owner.** Both cards keep complete proofs. I.7.7(b) is proved without the induction: blowing up the nonsingular point $P$, the resolved projection $\widetilde\rho:\widetilde Y\to Z$ onto the cone's base $Z$ is generically finite of some degree $\delta\ge1$, and $\widetilde\rho^*\OO_Z(1)\cong\OO_{\widetilde Y}(\beta^*H-E)$ gives $(\beta^*H-E)^r=\delta\deg Z$, while $(\beta^*H-E)^r=H^r+(-1)^rE^r=d-1$ because $E\cong\PP^{r-1}$ with normal bundle $\OO(-1)$; hence $\deg X=\deg Z=(d-1)/\delta\le d-1$. I.7.8 is then completed by codimension one in $L\cong\PP^{r+1}$: the homogeneous coordinate ring of $L$ is a unique factorization domain, so the prime ideal of $Y$ is generated by one irreducible homogeneous form, of degree $2$ by I.7.6(d).

**Uncertainty.** Searched: all twelve retained Hartshorne solution files in `tmp/sources` by `pdftotext -layout` extraction — Borcherds, Cais, Cutrone--Marshburn, Egbert, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Park, Saglam--Chris, Sam, Stein, Troiani — and `assets/attachments/Hartshorne_Solutions.pdf`, recorded by its provenance file as a byte-identical duplicate of the Cais notes. Found: Chapter I §7 material only in Borcherds (PDF pp. 9--10), Egbert (PDF pp. 55--58) and Cutrone--Marshburn (PDF pp. 25--27). Troiani's Chapter I stops at §5; Park's at §1; Sam's Chapter I, after reversing its mirrored text layer line by line, at §4; Cais, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Saglam--Chris and Stein begin at Chapter II. Conclusion: no complete published solution for I.7.7(b) or for the quadric half of I.7.8. Confidence: high for these sets. Gaps: a published treatment may exist outside them, and I.7.7(a) itself has adequate published arguments.

**Repair.** A published proof of each, checked against the card, or the owner's direction to accept the cards' own derivations.

**Searched outside the retained sets (issue #131, 2026-11-11).** Neither was closed. For I.7.7(b) the only outside statement found is R. Hartshorne, "Varieties of small codimension in projective space", *Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society* 80 (1974), which states that a variety of dimension $r$ and degree $d$ in $\PP^n$ lies in a linear space $\PP^{r+d-1}$ and attributes it to "an elementary argument"; it was read as a search excerpt only, not consulted, and it does not prove the degree drop. For the quadric half of I.7.8 nothing outside the retained sets proves that a variety of degree two is a hypersurface of its span; Mat Kerr's notes classify quadrics inside a fixed $\PP^n$ only. The card's own proofs were read: for I.7.7(b) the blowup identity $(\beta^*H-E)^r=H^r+(-1)^rE^r=d-1$ with $E^r=(-1)^{r-1}$, which is computed for $r\ge1$ and needs no separate case $\dim Y=0$, that case being excluded by $d>1$ (this paragraph recorded it as missing and as supplied by a step of the card; the step was vacuous and is removed, see the note of 2026-11-16 under this entry); for I.7.8 the principal height-one prime of $k[x_0,\ldots,x_{r+1}]$ and its degree $2$ by I.7.6(d) (printed p. 52).

**Searched again, 2026-11-16, and what the nearest statements do and do not do.**

(i) A. Dolgachev, *Topics in Classical Algebraic Geometry* (27 September 2010), the complete 524-page treatise at `tmp/sources/dolgachev-topics-classical-ag.pdf`, Theorem 8.1.1 on printed p. 247 (PDF p. 257; printed $=$ PDF $-10$), states: for an irreducible nondegenerate $X\subseteq\PP^n$ of dimension $k$ and degree $d$, "$d\ge n-k+1$, and the equality holds only in one of the following cases: (i) $X$ is an irreducible quadric hypersurface; (ii) a Veronese surface; (iii) a cone over a Veronese surface; (iv) a rational normal scroll". With $d=2$ that would give the span half of I.7.8 at once, and its equality case (i) the quadric half, in the span of $Y$. It is, however, stated without proof: the text says "We have the following well-known (i.e., can be found in modern text-books, e.g. [197], [203]) result", and those are P. Griffiths and J. Harris, *Principles of algebraic geometry* and J. Harris, *Algebraic geometry. A first course*. Neither is retained and no accessible copy was consulted, so this is a published statement, not a published argument. Dolgachev's Chapter 8 says nothing about I.7.7(b).

(ii) Math Stack Exchange question 3038470, *Degree and codimension of nondegenerate varieties*, asks for exactly the proof of that inequality as it is given "in the paper *On Varieties of Minimal Degree* by Eisenbud and Harris", namely why a general projection from a point of $X$ lowers both the degree and the codimension; read through the API on 2026-11-16 it has no answers. So the inequality itself is not available in argued form there either.

(iii) Miles Reid, *Chapters on Algebraic Surfaces*, printed p. 22 (PDF p. 22 of the retained copy, whose PDF page is its printed page), text version `tmp/sources/reid-chapters-algebraic-surfaces.md`, states the same theorem under del Pezzo's name: "an irreducible $d$-dimensional variety $V$ spanning $\PP^n$ has degree $\ge n-d+1$, and if equality holds then $V$ is a linearly embedded scroll ..., a cone over a scroll ..., or one of the sporadic cases: $\PP^n$ itself, a quadric hypersurface $Q\subset\PP^n$, the Veronese surface $W\subset\PP^5$ or a cone over $W$. See [Bertini] or Eisenbud and Harris [E--H] for proofs of different vintages, or do it for yourself (Ex. 2.19)." So the third located statement defers the proof too, to the same paper or to an exercise of its own book, and none of the three proves it. For I.7.8 the case $d=2$ is exactly Reid's sporadic case "quadric hypersurface $Q\subset\PP^n$", which is the conclusion the exercise wants.

(iv) D. Eisenbud and J. Harris, *On varieties of minimal degree (a centennial account)*, Proceedings of Symposia in Pure Mathematics 46 (1987), is the paper both (i) and (ii) send the reader to. It is not in `tmp/sources` and no accessible copy was obtained in this pass; the 1981 Harris paper *A bound on the geometric genus of projective varieties* (Numdam), which states the same monodromy input for curves, does not contain the inequality.

(v) The precise published location of the inequality is named in print. D. Eisenbud, M. Green, K. Hulek and S. Popescu, *The geometry of 2-regular algebraic sets* (arXiv:math/0404517, version 3 of 9 June 2004), introduction: "Any variety $X\subset\PP^r$ satisfies the condition $\deg(X)\ge\codim(X,\operatorname{span}(X))+1$ (see for instance Mumford [1976, Corollary 5.13])", its Theorem being the del Pezzo--Bertini classification. So the proof is Mumford, *Algebraic Geometry I: Complex Projective Varieties*, Corollary 5.13, which is the reference Dolgachev, Reid and the Stack Exchange question all fall short of naming. Mumford's book is not retained and no accessible copy was obtained; the corollary was not read, so nothing from it is transcribed here. The quoted sentence was read in the retained PDF `tmp/sources/eisenbud-green-hulek-popescu-2-regular-sets.pdf`; `tmp/sources` holds no text version of that file.

(vi) The same authors' journal paper reaches the inequality for reducible sets and again defers its proof. D. Eisenbud, M. Green, K. Hulek and S. Popescu, *Small schemes and varieties of minimal degree*, Theorem 1.4(a) on its PDF p. 6 states, for an equidimensional reduced projective scheme $X$ connected in codimension 1 with span $L$, that $\deg X\ge\codim(X,L)+1$, and its proof reads: "Part (a) of Theorem 1.4 is elementary: the proof works as in the irreducible case (see Hartshorne [1962]) using the connectedness hypothesis to guarantee that the plane section is nondegenerate." The bibliography identifies Hartshorne [1962] as R. Hartshorne, *Complete intersections and connectedness*, Amer. J. Math. 84 (1962). So the irreducible case is referred in print to a paper, and the paper is not on this machine. The copy is saved at `tmp/sources/eisenbud-green-hulek-popescu-small-schemes-minimal-degree.pdf`, and `tmp/sources` holds no text version of it either, so the quoted sentence was read in that PDF at PDF p. 6.

(vii) Re-read this pass in their text versions, to confirm what the entries above say they do: Richard E. Borcherds, Exercise 7.7, PDF pp. 9--10, `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-borcherds.md`, whose 7.7(b) is the induction with the unproved identity $\deg X=\deg(X\cap H)$ and whose own note concedes that $X\cap H$ need not be irreducible; and A. Neither proves the degree drop, and neither states the quadric half.

**Conclusion for this pass.** I.7.7(b) keeps its blow-up computation and the quadric half of I.7.8 keeps its unique-factorization argument. **Correction, 2026-11-16, on the reader's report of #121.** Step `zero-dimensional-case` of `P-AGH77CONEDEGDROP` was vacuous and has been removed. The exercise's $Y$ is a variety, so it is irreducible, $\dim Y=0$ makes it a single point of degree $1$, and $d>1$ excludes that case; the step's "$d$ points, $X$ a union of lines" describes an algebraic set, which is what Borcherds, Egbert and Cutrone--Marshburn treat when they open their inductions there. The hypothesis $r\ge1$ that the blow-up step uses is now stated in that step, from irreducibility of $Y$ and Proposition I.7.6(a); the earlier claim in this entry and in the card that the case was "missing" was false. Two other statements of this entry are now explicit rather than implied: the quadric half of I.7.8 uses I.7.6(d) for the degree of $Y$ *in* $L\cong\PP^{r+1}$, and the card now says why that equals $\deg Y$ as a subvariety of $\PP^n$ (the homogeneous coordinate rings coincide after a linear change of coordinates); and the two EGHP citations in (v) and (vi) name their PDFs and record that `tmp/sources` holds no text version of either.

**Correction, 2026-11-16, on the reader's report of #121: the I.7.7(b) entry.** The paragraph above was rewritten in place by commit `89d13d01e1` and is restored here to the text it had on its date. Its content stands except for one citation, which this entry corrects: the hypothesis $r\ge1$ of the blow-up step does not come from Proposition I.7.6(a) for the *value* of the degree. That proposition says only that the degree of a nonempty $Y$ in $\PP^n$ is a positive integer; a point has degree $1$ because its Hilbert polynomial is the constant $1$, and $0!=1$. Step `blowup-resolves-projection` of `P-AGH77CONEDEGDROP` and its 2026-11-16 event say so.

**2026-11-16: I.7.7(b) is closed on Mumford's Proposition 2.5 and Harris's Example 18.16.** `P-AGH77CONEDEGDROP` now proves the degree drop from two printed statements and no longer from its own blow-up. Harris, *Algebraic Geometry: A First Course* (1992), Example 18.16, printed pp. 234--235, gives the degree of the cone over a variety as the degree of the base (printed p. 234), which with the projection from $P$ identifies $\deg X$ with $\deg Z$ for the base $Z$ of the cone, and gives $\deg(\overline X)=\deg(X)-1$ for the projection of a variety from one of its smooth points (printed p. 235). Mumford, *Stability of projective varieties*, L'Enseignement Mathématique 23 (1977), printed p. 55, gives the same count without Harris's standing assumption that the general line through $p$ meets $X$ only at $p$ and at one more point: Definition 2.2 defines $e_L(\mathcal I)$ as the normalized leading coefficient of $\chi(L^n/\mathcal I^nL^n)$, his examples after it identify that number with the Hilbert-Samuel multiplicity at the point when the base locus is a point, and Proposition 2.5 states $e_L(\mathcal I_A)=\deg X-\deg p_A(X)$. Applied with $A$ the hyperplanes through $P$, whose base locus on $Y$ is $\{P\}$, this gives $d=\deg Y=\deg p_A(Y)+1\ge\deg Z+1$, whence $\deg X=\deg Z\le d-1$. Text versions `tmp/sources/harris-1992-algebraic-geometry-first-course-pp224-243.md` and `tmp/sources/mumford-1977-stability-projective-varieties.md`. **The one step that no single source prints:** that $e_L(\mathcal I_A)=1$ at a nonsingular point. Mumford says only that $e_L$ is the multiplicity there, and Harris says only that a general $r$-tuple of hyperplanes through a smooth point of a variety meets it transversely at that point (printed p. 235); the card puts the two together and the step says so. Part (a) is unchanged and keeps its tangent-space route for $\dim X>r$, with KReiser's accepted answer 4656385 (question 4656099, cited by answer id) named for the two bounds it shares and for the induction on $\dim Y$ that it carries out. The blow-up computation is now a remark on the card rather than its proof, with its $(\beta^*H-E)^r=d-1=\delta\deg Z$ and the reasons for each term.

**Correction, 2026-11-16, on the reader's report of #121: the I.7.7(b) entry restored.** This record is one of the four restored in the I.3.16 entry, for the reason given there, and it is set off from the correction paragraph before it by the blank line the edit that added them both left out, so that it reads as the record it is. Borcherds, *Hartshorne, Chapter 1: Answers to exercises* (1994), Exercise 7.6, PDF p. 9, text version `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-borcherds.md`, transcribed on the card rather than cited by number: a hyperplane section of a degree-one variety has degree one by the Bézout theorem of Hartshorne printed p. 53, is linear by induction on the ambient dimension, and the variety, being closed under joins of its points, equals its linear span. ### V.1.11(a) and (b) of `SRC-TEXT-HART77` have no complete published solution; V.1.4(b) and the surface example of V.1.12 closed on transcriptions

**Object and need.** Two parts of one request in `SRC-TEXT-HART77` §V.1 are proved on the card without a published argument to check against, parts (a) and (b) of V.1.11; when this entry was opened it was three cards, and the other two are closed below: `P-AGH514LINEONSURF` (V.1.4(b), printed p. 367, PDF p. 382, a nonsingular degree-$d$ surface through a given line, every $d\ge1$), `P-AGH5111FINITEAUT` (V.1.11(a) and (b), printed p. 368, PDF p. 383, finiteness of the numerical classes of effective divisors with $D\cdot H=d$, and of the automorphisms modulo the identity component) and `P-AGH5112NUMAMPLE` (V.1.12, printed p. 368, PDF p. 383, a very ample $D$ numerically equivalent to a non-very-ample $D'$).

**Observed evidence.** For all of Chapter V the only retained set that reaches the section is Andrew Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (October 3, 2013), PDF pp. 254--261 for V.1; Park's *Exercises solutions* has Chapter V §5 only (PDF p. 31), Borcherds stops at Chapter I, and Cais, Cutrone--Marshburn, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Saglam--Chris, Stein and Troiani have no Chapter V. Egbert's V.1.4(b) reads "The fermat hypersurface $x^d+y^d+z^d+w^d=0$ contains the line $x-\sqrt[n]{\ }$" and breaks off inside the formula, so his entry is truncated and exhibits no surface at all; on that hypersurface the lines $x=\zeta y$, $z=\zeta w$ with $\zeta^d=-1$ lie on it in every degree, and only the line $x+y=z+w=0$ lies on it solely for odd $d$, since $x^d+(-x)^d=2x^d$ in even degree. His V.1.11(a) is "WLOG assume that $H$ is a very ample hyperplane of $\deg(H)=1$. For $D\cdot H=0$ this follows from nakai moishezon. Note that any such $D$ can only have finitely many components not intersecting $H$ since if $P_i\cdot H=0$, then $P_i\cdot P_j<0$ and with each additional such component, the genus, $2g-2=C\cdot C+C\cdot K\ge-2$ will decrease. ... Thus we are choosing $D$ from a finite set of a finite number of components": the components meeting $H$ and the coefficients $n_i$ are never bounded, and $P_i\cdot P_j<0$ is asserted. His V.1.12 reduces the curve case correctly and then writes "Consider a decomposable ruled surface $X$ over a curve with $p_a(C)>2$, let $H=|C_0+bf|$ ... By Fuentes-Pedreira thm 3.9, $|H|$ is very ample iff $b$ and $b+e$ are very ample": that criterion is retained now and is the right one for a decomposable surface, but he fixes no value of $e$ and never verifies that $b+e$ is very ample, so his surface example is a citation rather than an exhibit.

**Impact and owner.** The cards keep complete proofs: V.1.4(b) now carries the National Taiwan University surface $x^{d-1}z+xz^{d-1}+y^{d-1}w+yw^{d-1}$, whose partial derivatives have no common projective zero in characteristic zero, for every $d$, with the case analysis its source omits; V.1.11(a) bounds the $H^\perp$ component of every irreducible curve by adjunction and $p_a\ge0$, then uses that $\Num X$ is a lattice in $\Num X\otimes\RR$, and finally writes an effective divisor as a sum of at most $d$ elements of a finite set; V.1.12 takes $C\times\PP^1$ with $M=p_1^*L\otimes p_2^*\OO(1)$ very ample and $M'=p_1^*L'\otimes p_2^*\OO(1)$ not very ample for $L'=K_C(P+Q)$, whose difference pulls back from a degree-zero bundle on $C$, and Fuentes--Pedreira's Theorem 3.9(3) decides both. What is missing is a published argument for V.1.11(a).

**Uncertainty.** Searched: all twelve retained Hartshorne solution files in `tmp/sources` by `pdftotext -layout` extraction, plus `assets/attachments/Hartshorne_Solutions.pdf` (the Cais notes, recorded as a byte-identical duplicate by its provenance file). Found: Chapter V only in Egbert (V.1 at PDF pp. 254--261, V.2--V.6 at pp. 261 onward) and in Park for V.5 alone. Sam's mirrored text layer was reversed line by line and carries no Chapter V. Conclusion: no complete published solution for the three requests above among these sets. Confidence: high for these sets. Gaps: a published treatment may exist outside them.

The page numbers in this entry were the PDF pages of the extraction; the printed pages are 367 and 368.

**Verified and transcribed (2026-11-16, corrected 2026-11-16).** The treatments were re-read in their text versions and checked line by line against the book. `P-AGH514LINEONSURF` carries the published argument rather than a parallel one: step `s3` uses the National Taiwan University set's $x^{d-1}z+xz^{d-1}+y^{d-1}w+yw^{d-1}$ in place of the card's earlier $xz^{d-1}+yw^{d-1}+x^d+y^d$, and step `s4` solves that set's four equations, which it states without solution. The solution is complete: the four partial derivatives are $2z$, $2x$, $2w$, $2y$ when $d=2$; for $d\ge3$, $z=0$ forces $x=0$ from the derivative in $z$, while $z\ne0$ turns $(d-1)x^{d-2}=-z^{d-2}$ and $x^{d-2}=-(d-1)z^{d-2}$ into $(d-1)^2=1$, which fails; and the same argument with $y,w$ replaces $x,z$. Characteristic zero enters only through the nonvanishing of $2$, $d-1$ and $(d-1)^2-1$. Two claims of the remark were wrong and are withdrawn: Egbert's V.1.4(b) sentence is truncated inside its formula, and the Fermat surface carries the lines $x=\zeta y$, $z=\zeta w$ with $\zeta^d=-1$ in every degree, only the line $x+y=z+w=0$ failing in even degree; and Yang Pi-Yeh's surface carries minus signs on its last two terms, so it is not the National Taiwan University set's surface.

`P-AGH5111FINITEAUT` and `P-AGH5112NUMAMPLE` keep proofs of their own, and neither is a transcription. For V.1.11 the National Taiwan University set's estimate $\sum_ic_i^2\le c_0^2+c_0k_0+2+\frac12k_0^2$ does not follow from its adjunction line, which bounds $\sum_i(c_i^2+c_ik_i)$ and reaches $\sum_ic_i^2$ only through $2\abs{c_ik_i}\le c_i^2+k_i^2$, and its (b) is the printed hint, which never proves that distinct automorphisms have numerically inequivalent graphs; the card's step `s8` supplies that step and nothing in `tmp/sources` does. For V.1.12 the card's steps `s6` and `s7` now run through Fuentes--Pedreira's criterion, with the card's direct product-embedding and fibre-restriction arguments kept beside them.

**V.1.12 closed on Fuentes--Pedreira.** Luis Fuentes and Manuel Pedreira, *The Projective Theory of Ruled Surfaces*, arXiv:math/0006204v3, text version `tmp/sources/projective-theory-ruled-surfaces.md` with its PDF `tmp/sources/projective-theory-ruled-surfaces.pdf`, Theorem 3.9(3), printed p. 18: on a decomposable ruled surface $|X_0+\mfb f|$ is very ample exactly when $\mfb$ and $\mfb+\mfe$ are. Write $X=C\times\PP^1$ as $\PP(\OO_C\oplus\OO_C)$, so that $e=0$, $X_0=C\times\{t\}$ and $f=\{c\}\times\PP^1$; then $p_1^*L\otimes p_2^*\OO(1)=X_0+Lf$, and the criterion decides the example in one step: very ampleness of $\mfb=L$ holds (the card's step `s3`) and that of $\mfb=L'=K_C(P+Q)$ fails (step `s4`). That is a complete published argument for the surface example, and it is the criterion Egbert cited without specializing. The criterion's proof rests on the paper's Corollary 2.13, printed p. 14, and that corollary is proved: its forward direction is Theorem 2.11, printed pp. 12--13, and its converse is Proposition 2.3, printed p. 8, applied to the system $|H-Pf|$ — a point at which the map fails is a base point of some $|H-Pf|$ by Theorem 2.11, and Proposition 2.3 produces $Q$ with $h^0(H-(P+Q)f)\ge h^0(H-Pf)-1=h^0(H)-3$ once $|H|$ is base-point-free. The case $Q=P$ is the tangent direction the earlier reading supposed untested. The defect this file and the V.2.12 card had recorded against Corollary 2.13, against Proposition 2.15 and against Theorem 3.9(3) is therefore withdrawn.


**Repair.** Discharged for V.1.4(b), on a transcription of the National Taiwan University set's Exercise 4, and for V.1.12, on Fuentes--Pedreira's Theorem 3.9(3) specialized to $C\times\PP^1$ with $e=0$. V.1.11(a) and (b) stay open: the National Taiwan University set's (a) estimate does not follow from its adjunction line and its (b) omits the step from finitely many numerical classes to finitely many automorphisms, so no complete published argument for either part has been located, and Yang Pi-Yeh bounds nothing in (a).

**2026-11-16, V.1.11: (b) closes on Bragg's Proof 2, and (a) still has no complete published proof.** The two sources named for this batch were read in their text versions on 2026-11-16: Math StackExchange answer 4775583 by KReiser, saved with its question as `tmp/sources/mse-4449474-hart-v111a-finite-automorphisms.md`, for (a); and Dan Bragg, "Automorphisms of curves" (2015), `tmp/sources/bragg-2015-automorphisms-of-curves.md`, Proof 2, "Intersection Theory", for (b). Bragg's Proof 2 is a complete published proof of (b) given (a): the graphs of distinct automorphisms are distinct irreducible curves, so they meet nonnegatively, while numerically equivalent graphs would meet in $\Gamma^2=2-2g<0$ by his conormal computation of the diagonal, hence $\sigma\mapsto[\Gamma_\sigma]$ is injective; and every graph meets the canonical divisor of $C\times C$ in the same $4g-4$, which he uses as the fixed ample divisor, ample for $g\ge2$ by Nakai--Moishezon since $K\cdot l=K\cdot m=2g-2>0$ and $K^2=2(2g-2)^2>0$. The card's steps `s6` to `s10` are that argument, so the step `s8` that the earlier record above says nothing in `tmp/sources` supplied is Bragg's. The answer 4775583's route to (a) is the card's, but two of its displays do not follow: its step from $-\sum_ib_i^2(D_i\cdot K+2)$ to $-d\,D\cdot K-2d^2$ replaces $b_i^2$ by $b_id$ under $D_i\cdot K$, which $b_i\le d$ licenses only when $D_i\cdot K\le0$ for every component and which fails on a surface with $K$ ample, and its closing sentence bounds $(D-E)^2$ below by an expression linear in $D$, so it describes no ellipsoid and yields no uniformity. Part (a) therefore stays open, and its bound stays the card's, through the orthogonal decomposition of $K_X$ in $H^\perp$ and the lattice $\Num X$. Uncertainty: whether a published treatment of (a) outside these two sources exists; the answer's own comment thread records that an earlier answer of its author had been withdrawn as insufficient.

**2026-11-16, V.1.11, corrected: two of the reasons recorded just above are withdrawn, and one case stays open.** The paragraph above records two failures of Math StackExchange answer 4775583. Both are wrong and are withdrawn on this date. First the direction: replacing $b_i^2$ by $b_id$ under $D_i\cdot K_X$ is the inequality $b_i^2D_i\cdot K_X\le db_iD_i\cdot K_X$, which follows from $b_i\le d$ when $D_i\cdot K_X\ge0$, not when it is at most $0$; the record has the sign the wrong way round, and the display is reached whenever $K_X$ is nef. Second the closing sentence: for fixed $E$ its right-hand side is an affine function of $D-E$, so with the intersection form negative definite on $H^\perp$ the inequality confines $D-E$ to a ball and finitely many lattice points follow; it need not depend on $E$ alone, and the record's "no ellipsoid" is wrong. What survives is one condition, now stated at the card's step `s3`: the comparison is reversed for a component $D_i$ with $D_i\cdot K_X<0$ and $b_i<d$, so that display is not reached on such a surface, and no published argument for that case was located. The card's step `s4` is its own and gives the uniform bound without the sign condition; steps `s1`, `s2`, `s3`, `s5`, `s6`, `s7` now say which are the answer's and which are the card's. Two further corrections of this round on the same card: adjunction for a possibly singular effective divisor is Exercise V.1.3(a), printed p. 366, and for a nonsingular curve Proposition V.1.5, printed p. 361, not Theorem V.1.3, which is on printed p. 358; Bragg's Proof 2 has two paragraphs, so the card's locators are the first and the second; and "both degrees being at least one" is corrected to their sum, the projection being constant on a ruling. **Open for V.1.11(a):** the case of a surface with a component of negative $K_X$-degree, which the published answer does not reach and the card proves as its own.

### §V.2 of `SRC-TEXT-HART77`: four cards still have no complete published solution, and two more have a partial one

**Object and need.** Ten requests in `SRC-TEXT-HART77` §V.2 were proved on their cards without a complete published argument to check them against, and the per-card bullets below record where each now stands; the ten were: `P-AGH521BASEUNIQUE` (V.2.1, printed p. 383), `P-AGH522DECOMPSECT` (V.2.2, p. 383), `P-AGH523SUCCEXT` (V.2.3, pp. 383--384), `P-AGH525INVARIANTE` (V.2.5(a) and (c), p. 384), `P-AGH528STABLEBUNDLE` (V.2.8(c), p. 384), `P-AGH5210CANONSCROLL` (V.2.10, p. 385), `P-AGH5212ELLRULEDAMPLE` (V.2.12, p. 385), `P-AGH5213ELLSCROLL` (V.2.13, p. 385), `P-AGH5215FROBENIUSRULED` (V.2.15(c), p. 385) and `P-AGH5217CONORMALSPLIT` (V.2.17, p. 386).

**Observed evidence.** For Chapter V the retained sets are Andrew Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (October 3, 2013), PDF pp. 261--273 for §V.2, and Jinhyun Park's *Algebraic Geometry by Robin Hartshorne, Exercises solutions*, whose Chapter V is §V.5 alone and begins at the section cover page after his §IV.1; Borcherds, Cais, Cutrone--Marshburn, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Saglam--Chris, Sam, Stein and Troiani have no Chapter V. What Egbert has: V.2.1 is two lines, "Suppose that $C_0\times\PP^1\cong X\cong C_1\times\PP^1$. But two curves which are birational are isomorphic", asserting rather than proving the birationality of the bases; V.2.2 is the citation "Marumaye, Remark 1.20"; V.2.3(a) is the citation "Miyanishi, Algebraic Geometry Lemma 12.1", and his adjacent Chern-class computation is for the tangent bundle $T_{\PP^2}$ ($d_1+d_2=3$, $d_1d_2=3$, discriminant $-3$) rather than the sheaf of differentials the exercise names; V.2.5(a) ends "This is F,P thm 4.12.4" and (c) is "given by 3.13 in Maruyama"; V.2.8(c) runs a Harder--Narasimhan filtration, cites Potier for uniqueness, and concludes "Since the filtration was unique we have this up to isomorphism" without noticing that the maximal destabilizing subbundle, and hence the tensor twist, is not part of the data; V.2.10 is "See example 2.10 in Kollar's Complex Algebraic Geometry"; V.2.12 is "This is Fuentes, Pedreira Prop 1.3" and "Fuentes, Predeira prop 1.4"; V.2.13's dimension count reads $h^0=2n-1=d-1$, dropping $e$; V.2.15(c) is "To see the curve $Y\equiv3C_0-3f$ is inseparable is Miyanishi, *Open Algebraic Surfaces*, lemma 2.5.2.2"; V.2.17 is entered as "starred" with no argument. Fuentes--Pedreira, Maruyama, Miyanishi and Kollár are not among the retained files.

**Impact and owner.** The cards keep complete proofs: V.2.1 descends through the generic $\PP^1$-fibre and recovers inverse birational maps of the bases; V.2.2 compares the kernel line bundles of the two quotient sections fibrewise; V.2.3 filters a rank-$r$ bundle by saturation of a generic section; V.2.5(a) uses $H^1(\OO_C(K_C-A))^\vee\cong H^0(\OO_C(A))\ne0$ and (c) counts the bad extension classes in $\PP H^1(\OO_C(-D))$ as at most $2d-3$ against $g+d-2$; V.2.8(c) classifies up to tensor equivalence; V.2.10 constructs the canonical curve as $D=H-K_X\sim3C_0+(n+e+2)f$; V.2.12 handles $e\ge0$ and the exceptional $e=-1$ separately, the latter through the stability of a normalized bundle of degree one; V.2.13 gets $h^0=2n-e=d$ and the scroll in $\PP^{d-1}$; V.2.15(c) builds $Y$ from the splitting of $f^*\mathcal E$; V.2.17 computes the extension class $(n-1)\eta$ of the conormal sequence and reproduces the book's printed answers $-5$, $-7$ and $(-6,-8)$ in characteristic $2$. Two of these cards also carry a defect in the printed text, recorded on the card: V.2.8(c)'s "up to isomorphism" fails because $\mathcal E$ and $\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal A$ with $\deg\mathcal A\ne0$ carry the same triple $(e,\mathcal L,\xi)$ and have different determinants, and V.2.15(c)'s "nonsingular" fails because adjunction gives $p_a(3C_0-3f)=4$ while a purely inseparable degree-three cover of the genus-three curve has genus $3$.

**Uncertainty.** Searched: all twelve retained Hartshorne solution files in `tmp/sources` by `pdftotext -layout` extraction --- Borcherds, Cais, Cutrone--Marshburn, Egbert, Kim, Lomont, Okamoto, Park, Saglam--Chris, Sam, Stein, Troiani --- and `assets/attachments/Hartshorne_Solutions.pdf`, the Cais notes. The Chapter V occurrences in Cutrone--Marshburn, Kim, Saglam--Chris and Lomont are all in Chapter II material on blowing up, with one cross-reference to "geometrically ruled surface (V, §2)" in Kim. Conclusion: no complete published solution for the ten requests above. Confidence: high for these sets. Gaps: a published treatment may exist outside them.

**Located sources.** Algebraic Geometry II, National Taiwan University, 2020 Spring (course of Chin-Lung Wang), *Chapter V Surfaces* homework, in `tmp/sources/ntu-ag2-chapter5.md` beside its PDF, covers five of the ten with arguments: V.2.1 (Exercise 1 of §2, PDF p. 5), V.2.2 (Exercise 2, PDF pp. 5--6), V.2.3 (Exercise 3, PDF p. 6), V.2.8 (Exercise 8, PDF p. 8, whose (c) is a citation to the proof of 2.12), V.2.10 (Exercise 10, PDF p. 8), and it has no entry for V.2.5, V.2.12, V.2.13, V.2.15 or V.2.17. Yang Pi-Yeh, *Hartshorne Solutions* (`tmp/sources/lfwin-hartshorne-solutions.pdf`, 2019), gives printed pp. 101--107: V.2.1 by $K(X)=L(x)$ (which assumes what the exercise proves), V.2.2 by two assertions, V.2.3 with a sign error in (b), V.2.5 with an invalid inference from nonnegative degree in (a), V.2.8 repeating the printed "up to isomorphism", V.2.10 without nonsingularity or canonicity, V.2.12 with garbled $e=-1$ computations, V.2.13 correctly, V.2.15 with the (a) computation and garbled (b) and (c), and V.2.17 by the Jacobian presentation but with characteristic 3 wrongly added to the split case. The cards now record, per exercise, which published argument exists and where it fails; V.2.4, V.2.6, V.2.7, V.2.9, V.2.11 and V.2.14, whose Egbert entries are complete, were not in this batch.



**Searched outside the retained sets (2026-11-16).** Two further published sources were read for this batch. Luis Fuentes and Manuel Pedreira, *The Projective Theory of Ruled Surfaces*, arXiv:math/0006204v3 (2002), was saved whole as `tmp/sources/projective-theory-ruled-surfaces.pdf`; its §2 proves base-point and very-ampleness criteria for the linear system of $C_0+\mfb f$ and its §3 treats decomposable ruled surfaces. Math StackExchange threads were read through the API and are cited below by question and answer id. Per card:

- V.2.1. Fuentes--Pedreira Proposition 1.7, printed p. 5, builds the incidence variety of a linearly normal scroll and concludes that the scroll determines its ruled surface; that is uniqueness of the ruling of an embedded scroll, not the birational uniqueness this exercise asks for, so it does not reach the exercise. Math StackExchange question 1715815, saved whole as `tmp/sources/mse-1715815-hart77-v21-uniqueness-of-ruling.md`, asks the isomorphism form --- if $C_1\times\PP^1\cong C_2\times\PP^1$, show $C_1\cong C_2$ --- which is strictly weaker than the birational statement here. It has no answer and four comments, the saved file now holding all of them: Mohan's sketch through $C_1\times\{p\}\to C_2$, with the genus read off $h^1$ of the product, the rational case, Hurwitz for genus above one, and a remark that genus one needs an extra argument; the poster's question whether that last step is Hurwitz's theorem; Mohan's confirmation that it is; and Takumi Murayama's pointers to Ohm following Nagata and to Deveney, with his remark that Mohan's argument covers the birational case too. The Ohm and Deveney pointers are Murayama's and not Mohan's, which is the one thing the earlier record got wrong; that the thread is a sketch in a comment and not a published argument stands, so the published argument remains the National Taiwan University set's. Chao Li's Columbia notes, "Enriques classification of complex algebraic surfaces", were read as well: Theorem 7 and its proof show that every minimal model of $C\times\PP^1$ with $C$ irrational is geometrically ruled over $C$, which recovers the base from a minimal model but never states that $C$ is determined by the birational class. The complete published argument is the National Taiwan University set's Exercise 1 of §2, printed p. 5, whose two cases are steps `s2` to `s4` of the card; its last case, "if $C=\PP^1$ then $\widetilde f$ is a constant, which means $f$ is a constant, a contradiction", is valid, and the earlier record that it was invalid is withdrawn: a constant $\widetilde f$ confines the image of the birational map to one fibre of $p'$, a curve.
- V.2.2. Fuentes--Pedreira Remark 3.3, printed p. 15, is the conclusion in one sentence, two disjoint unisecant curves coming from the two summands, with neither direction proved; its Theorem 3.2, printed p. 15, cites the book's Theorem V.2.12 and Nagata and concerns only the possible values of $e$. The National Taiwan University set is a complete published treatment of both directions, but it is not the card's argument: it reads $\Rightarrow$ off $C_1\cdot C_2=0$ and $\Leftarrow$ off $\pi^*$ with the flatness and surjectivity of $\pi$, where steps `s1` and `s3` of the card use the fibres of $\mathcal E$ and the determinant.
- V.2.3. Nothing in Fuentes--Pedreira. The book's own Corollary V.2.7, printed p. 372 (PDF p. 387), proves the rank-two case of (a) completely, and Remark V.2.7.1 on the same printed page sends the general rank to this exercise. Part (b) does have a complete published argument, the National Taiwan University set's Exercise 3 of §2, printed p. 6: an extension $0\to\OO(n)\to\Omega\to\OO(m)\to0$ forces $H^1(\PP^2,\Omega)=0$ by III.5.1(b), printed p. 225, against $H^1(\PP^2,\Omega)\cong k$ from the Euler sequence. Steps `s3` and `s4` of the card are its own Chern-class route to the same contradiction; step `s1` is likewise its own, starting from $\mathcal E(n)$ rather than the set's $\mathcal E^\vee(n)$.
- V.2.5. Fuentes--Pedreira Theorem 3.2, printed p. 15, restates the book's Theorem V.2.12, printed p. 376, with a sharper lower bound: the book prints $e\ge0$ in the decomposable case and $-2g\le e\le2g-2$ in the indecomposable one, which is what its own proof yields, and sends the sharper $e\ge-g$ to its Exercise V.2.5, whose Note attributes it to Nagata [8]; the paper states the sharper bound and cites the book and Nagata for it. It says nothing about existence for every $e$ with $0\le e\le2g-2$, which is (a), nor about the range $-g\le e<0$, which is (c). Its Theorem 4.12(4), printed pp. 31--32, which Egbert cites for (a), is the paper's only construction of an indecomposable ruled surface: an elementary transformation of a decomposable surface at a point off $X_0$ and $X_1$, over a base point $P$ of the linear system of $-\mfe$, gives an indecomposable surface with invariant $e-1$. Applied once to the decomposable surface of invariant $e+1$, which exists for every $e\ge0$ by the book's Theorem V.2.12(a), it returns an indecomposable surface of invariant $e$, so no iteration is needed and the theorem covers every $0\le e\le2g-2$ as soon as a base point $P$ is produced; the paper leaves that to the reader, and it is available whenever $h^0(-\mfe)=1$, the system then having the single member $-\mfe$ whose support is its base locus. Part (a) therefore has a published argument modulo that one condition, and the card's steps `s1` to `s4` prove it without any condition. Math StackExchange question 4398506, saved as `tmp/sources/mse-4398506-hart77-v25-linear-system-notation.md`, concerns only the notation $\linearsystem{D+K-E}+E$ of part (b). No complete published argument for (c). Part (d) is open in this entry and is not proved on the card, whose step `s15` records the printed Note and the reference to Nagata rather than deriving the bound, the book's own argument reaching only $e\ge-2g$, that is $e\ge-4$ at $g=2$: it needs Nagata's $e\ge-g$, which the printed Note, Fuentes--Pedreira's introduction and its Theorem 3.2(2) all attribute to M. Nagata, "On self-intersection number of a section on a ruled surface", Nagoya Math. J. 37 (1970), 191--196 --- Hartshorne's own reference [8] and Fuentes--Pedreira's [15] --- and that paper was not read: Project Euclid serves an automated-access check for its PDF and Cambridge Core holds it for subscribers. An attempt to download it produced `tmp/sources/nagata-1970-self-intersection-section-ruled-surface.pdf`, which is not the paper --- it is 1157 bytes of Incapsula access-check HTML served under a .pdf name --- and no card cites that file. Step `s15` therefore rests on the printed Note and on two secondary statements of the bound.
- V.2.8(c). Nothing in Fuentes--Pedreira on stability of locally free sheaves on a curve. The printed "up to isomorphism" stays defective as recorded on the card.
- V.2.10. Fuentes--Pedreira §2 and §3 give criteria for the system of $C_0+\mfb f$ and never place a canonical curve on the rational scroll. Their §5 and §6 introduce "canonical surfaces" and "canonical scrolls" in the sense of scrolls of speciality one, deferring the characterization to their own "Canonical geometrically ruled surfaces", reference [5], which is not retained and was not read; that is not the canonical curve inside a rational scroll asked here. A search outside the checkout for a construction returned arXiv:1502.07556 and arXiv:1803.10899, both of which begin with a trigonal curve and study its canonical model rather than constructing one; Markwig and Zheng, "Trigonal and embedded tropical curves of low genus" (arXiv:2602.02257), read in its introduction, gives the class $3E_n+((g+3n+2)/2)F_n$ of a trigonal curve of genus $g$ and Maroni invariant $n$ and likewise begins with the curve. No complete published argument.
- V.2.12. Fuentes--Pedreira Theorem 3.9(3), printed p. 18, states for a decomposable ruled surface that the system of $C_0+\mfb f$ is very ample exactly when $\mfb$ and $\mfb+\mfe$ are; for $e\ge0$ on an elliptic base that gives $\deg\mfb\ge3$ and $\deg\mfb-e\ge3$, that is the printed bound $e+3$. That theorem is a complete published argument, and its proof is one too: it rests on the paper's Corollary 2.13, printed p. 14, whose criterion is $h^0(H-(P+Q)f)=h^0(H)-4$ for all $P,Q$ in the base, and that corollary is proved --- the forward direction by Theorem 2.11, printed pp. 12--13, and the converse by Proposition 2.3, printed p. 8, applied to $|H-Pf|$: a point at which the map fails is a base point of some $|H-Pf|$ by Theorem 2.11, and Proposition 2.3 then produces $Q$ with $h^0(H-(P+Q)f)\ge h^0(H-Pf)-1=h^0(H)-3$ once $|H|$ is base-point-free. The earlier record in this file, and on the card, that the converse was an assertion and that a two-fibre condition cannot see a tangent direction transverse to a fibre is withdrawn: the case $Q=P$ is what Theorem 2.11 covers. Proposition 2.15, printed p. 15, rests on the same corollary and is sound on the same footing. What the paper leaves open is what its Section 3, being about decomposable surfaces, does not reach: the Atiyah surface $e=-1$, handled by the card's `s8` and `s9`, and the indecomposable bundles of invariant $e=0$, handled by `s7` and `s10` through the book's Exercise V.2.11(b), which needs no decomposability.
- V.2.13. Fuentes--Pedreira's introduction cites the classification of elliptic scrolls of Corrado Segre, its reference [17] --- Segre, Ricerche sulle rigate ellittiche di qualunque ordine, Atti Acc. Torino 21 (1885), 868--891, not retained and not read --- and says that that classification does not follow directly from the very-ampleness criterion. The paper's own reference [4], the authors' "The classification of elliptic scrolls", appears only in its bibliography and is never cited in its text. What the paper does settle is every $e\ge0$ on a decomposable surface: Theorem 3.2(1), printed p. 15 (every $e\ge0$ occurs), Theorem 3.9(3), printed p. 18 (very ampleness), and Theorem 3.10(1), printed p. 19 ($N=h^0(\mfb)+h^0(\mfb+\mfe)-1$, degree $2\deg\mfb-e$). Only $e=-1$, the Atiyah surface, is open there, its bundles being indecomposable; the card's `s1` and its `s3` to `s7` carry that case, and Yang Pi-Yeh's count agrees with the card's.
- V.2.15(c). Fuentes--Pedreira carries no Frobenius statement. Question 4553266, saved as `tmp/sources/mse-4553266-hart77-v215c-genus-inseparable.md`, asks for the genus of exactly the curve of (c) and has no answer. Miyanishi, *Open Algebraic Surfaces*, Lemma 2.5.2.2, carried by Egbert's entry, is not retained and was not read. No complete published argument, and the defect of the printed "nonsingular" recorded on the card stands.
- V.2.17. Part (a) has a complete published argument: Math StackExchange answer 1583486 by Ted Shifrin, to question 1583326, in `tmp/sources/mse-1583326-hart77-v217-twisted-cubic-normal-bundle.md`, computes the conormal bundle of the twisted cubic by transition functions in the two charts and reads off $\OO(-5)\oplus\OO(-5)$; the transition matrix, the change of coordinates its answer leaves to the reader, and its reduction to $t^{-5}$ times the identity are now carried in step `s5` of the card. Equivalently the normal bundle is $\OO(5)\oplus\OO(5)$, which answer 569653 to question 569237, in `tmp/sources/mse-569237-hart77-v217-twisted-cubic-normal-bundle-2.md`, records as Proposition 6 of Eisenbud and Van de Ven. Answer 2664944 to question 2664333, in `tmp/sources/mse-2664333-hart77-v217-conormal-sheaf-twisted-cubic.md`, reaches the conormal sequence and the Jacobian matrix and stops at "it is easy to check that the conormal sheaf is $\OO(-5)$ squared", which the degree does not give, since $4(-3)-2(-1)=-10$ admits $\OO(-4)\oplus\OO(-6)$ as well. No published treatment of (b) or of its characteristic-two answer was located, and steps `s2` and `s3` remain the card's own general computation for both parts.

**Where this batch stands.** Complete published arguments are now recorded on six of the ten, and on part (a) alone of a seventh: V.2.1 through the National Taiwan University set, whose last case is valid; V.2.2 and V.2.3 through that set, by routes other than the cards' own; V.2.12 and V.2.13 through Fuentes--Pedreira for every $e\ge0$ on a decomposable surface, whose Theorem 3.9(3) and Corollary 2.13 are complete; and V.2.17 on part (a) through the two Stack Exchange answers. Two of these are partial: V.2.12 leaves the Atiyah surface $e=-1$ and the indecomposable bundles of invariant $e=0$ outside the published argument, and V.2.13 leaves $e=-1$ outside it, both of which the cards' own steps supply. The four without a complete published argument are V.2.5, whose (a) the paper gives only up to the base point its own theorem asks for and which the card proves outright, whose (c) is the card's, and whose (d) rests on Nagata's paper, unread; V.2.8(c), whose printed "up to isomorphism" is defective; V.2.10, where Fuentes--Pedreira's canonical surfaces are not the canonical curve inside a rational scroll; and V.2.15(c), whose printed "nonsingular" is defective.

**2026-11-16, §V.2: V.2.5 and V.2.10 close on published statements, V.2.8(c) on Gunning's Theorem 14, and the parts left open are named.** Seven sources named for this batch were read in their text versions on 2026-11-16 and transcribed onto the cards with the numbered statement and printed page of each step. V.2.5: part (a) is Gunning, *Lectures on vector bundles over Riemann surfaces*, Theorem 13, printed pp. 71--74 (extension classes are a first cohomology group, and the split extension is the zero class), and Theorem 14, printed pp. 87--90 (the indecomposable bundles with a given subbundle $\varphi$ and determinant $\xi$ are parametrized by $\PP H^1(C,\OO(\varphi^2\xi^{-1}))$), with the duality half of the book's proof of Theorem 2.12, printed p. 376, for the nonvanishing of $H^1(C,\mathcal L^{-1})$ at $\varphi=\OO_C$; part (b) is Proposition 1.1, printed p. 57, and Lemma 2.3, printed pp. 58--59, of Lange and Narasimhan, *Maximal subbundles of rank two vector bundles on curves*, Math. Ann. 266, whose criterion is the kernel of the canonical map $H^0(K_C\otimes L)^*\to H^0(K_C\otimes L(-D))^*$ in both directions, the same square the book's proof of Theorem 2.15, printed pp. 377--379, runs in one direction, and the printed "Cf. proof of (2.15)" points at; part (c) is their Corollary 1.2, printed p. 58, applied to line bundles of degrees $d$ and $2d$ with $d=-e$, since twisting by the inverse of the extension's subbundle returns a normalized bundle with determinant of degree $d$, with Example 2.11.6, printed p. 375, and Theorem 2.15 for genus one; and part (d) is Lange, *Higher secant varieties of curves and the theorem of Nagata on ruled surfaces*, Manuscripta Math. 47 (1984), §2 Theorem $s(E)\le g$, printed pp. 267--268, on the dimension theorem of §1, printed p. 266: for a normalized bundle $s(E)=\deg\det E=-e$, so $e\ge-g$ and $e\ge-2$ at $g=2$. That replaces the unread Nagata paper, which the printed Note and Fuentes--Pedreira both cite for the same bound. What stays open in part (d): the paper's proof reduces at its start to extensions whose quotient has degree $d>3$ and does not argue the reduction, while its §1 needs only $d\ge2$ when $g\ge2$. V.2.8(c): Gunning's §(c), printed pp. 82--83, Lemma 14, printed pp. 81--82, Lemma 15, printed pp. 83--85, and Theorem 14, printed pp. 87--90, are the stability criterion, the decomposable case, the uniqueness of the maximal subbundle and the classification with $\varphi=\OO_C$; the bound $0<e\le2g-2$ is the argument of the book's Theorem 2.12, printed p. 376. The printed "up to isomorphism" of the exercise remains defective, and the card classifies tensor-equivalence classes in terms of the printed data. V.2.10: Hartshorne's own Corollary 2.18(b), printed p. 380, states that $\linearsystem{D}$ contains an irreducible nonsingular curve exactly when $a>0$ and $b>ae$, or $e>0,a>0,b=ae$, and so covers $D=H-K_X=3C_0+(n+e+2)f$ under exactly the hypothesis $n\ge2e-2$ the exercise imposes; the proof of Corollary 2.19, printed p. 380, is the count $h^0(\OO_X(H))=2n-e+2$; and Reid, *Chapters on Algebraic surfaces*, §2.8 Theorem with (2.8.1), printed p. 19, §2.9, printed p. 20, and §2.10, printed pp. 20--21, give the class $\alpha A+3B$ with $\alpha=a+a_2+2$, the criterion $\alpha-3a=B\cdot(\alpha A+3B)\ge0$, and the Maroni inequality $3a\le g+2$ that is the same condition. The one step of that card not stated in either source is the restriction isomorphism $H^0(\OO_X(H))\cong H^0(Y,K_Y)$, which it assembles from the book's count with $H^0(\OO_X(K_X))=H^1(\OO_X(K_X))=0$. V.2.15(c) is untouched by this batch and stays open as recorded above.

**2026-11-16, §V.2, corrected: V.2.5(d) closes, V.2.5(b) and (c) gain the hypotheses of the statements they quote, and four records above are corrected.** Corrections of this round. (1) Hartshorne's Corollary 2.19 and its proof are on printed p. 381, not p. 380; the record above names p. 380 twice, and Corollary 2.18(b) keeps p. 380. (2) The adjunction formula in the V.2.10 card is Proposition V.1.5, printed p. 361, stated for a nonsingular curve, which is what the member $Y$ is; Theorem V.1.3 is the definition of the intersection number on printed p. 358. ### §V.3 of `SRC-TEXT-HART77`: six cards have no complete published solution

**Object and need.** Six requests in `SRC-TEXT-HART77` §V.3 are proved on their cards without a complete published argument to check them against: `P-AGH531PABLOWUP` (V.3.1, printed p. 394), `P-AGH534MULTLOCRING` (V.3.4(d) and (e), p. 394), `P-AGH535HYPERELLGENUS` (V.3.5, p. 394, the request to compute $\delta_P$), `P-AGH536ANALYTICEQUIV` (V.3.6, p. 395), `P-AGH537EMBRESOLUTION` (V.3.7, p. 395) and `P-AGH538INEQUIVSING` (V.3.8, p. 395).

**Observed evidence.** Andrew Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (October 3, 2013), PDF pp. 273--284 for §V.3, is the only retained set that reaches the section; Park's Chapter V is §V.5 alone, and the other ten retained sets stop before Chapter V. What Egbert has: V.3.1 is "This follows from 3.4", and result (3.4) is the monoidal case, a point centre, while the exercise blows up a subvariety of any codimension; V.3.4(d) is an unfinished attempt with a worked example $k[x,y]/(y^7-x^9)$ and no general argument, and V.3.4(e) is "See Mumford, Algebraic Geometry 1, Proposition 5.11"; V.3.5 checks the singularity at infinity and counts genus by Riemann--Hurwitz branch points but never computes $\delta_P$, which the exercise asks for; V.3.6 is "See Wall's, *Singular Points of Plane Curves*" for both halves, with the pair $y^3+x^7$ and $y^3+x^5y+x^7$ asserted equisingular but not analytically isomorphic; V.3.7 is a Singular session printing chart trees, with $\delta_P$ absent and the equivalence check left at "these commands should show that (d) is not equivalent"; V.3.8 says "the configuration of infinitely near singular points can be seen as in 3.7", asserts it rather than computing it, and observes only that (a) needs three charts and (b) four. Wall's book and Mumford's red book are not among the retained files.

**Impact and owner.** The cards keep complete proofs: V.3.1 reduces to $R^j\pi_*\OO_{\widetilde X}=0$ for a projective birational morphism of regular schemes (Chatzistamatiou--Rülling, Compositio Math. 151 (2015) 2131--2144, Theorem 1.1); V.3.4(d) computes $\length(\OO_{C,P}/\mathfrak m^l)=rl-r(r-1)/2$ from $\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m_C}\OO_{C,P}\cong k[u,v]/(f_r)$ and (e) gets the vertex multiplicity $d$ from the Hilbert polynomial of the cone's coordinate ring; V.3.5 gets $\delta_P=\binom{r-2}{2}+\lfloor(r-2)/2\rfloor$ from the strict transform $v^{r-2}=u^2\prod(1-a_iv)$ and the $A_{r-3}$ singularity its unit factor reduces to; V.3.6 proves the forward implication from the lifting of an analytic isomorphism to a formal coordinate change, and separates the standard pair by Tjurina numbers $12$ and $11$; V.3.7 gives the embedded resolutions and $\delta_P=4,4,3,4,4$; V.3.8 computes the multiplicity sequences. Two printed defects are recorded on the card: V.3.5 is printed without the hypothesis $\operatorname{char}k\ne2$ that its last two requests need (in characteristic $2$, $y^2=f(x)$ with $f$ squarefree is a purely inseparable double cover of genus $0$), and V.3.8 is false as printed, the two germs having multiplicity sequences $4,2$ and $4,3$ and $\delta_0=7$ and $9$, so they do not have the same infinitely near multiplicities and do have different delta invariants.

**Uncertainty.** Searched: all twelve retained Hartshorne solution files in `tmp/sources` by `pdftotext -layout` extraction, plus `assets/attachments/Hartshorne_Solutions.pdf` (the Cais notes). Chapter V occurs only in Egbert (V.1--V.6) and in Park (§V.5 alone). Conclusion: no complete published solution for the six requests above. Confidence: high for these sets. Gaps: a published treatment may exist outside them.

**Located sources.** Two published Chapter V solution sets outside the twelve previously inspected cover five of the six. Algebraic Geometry II, National Taiwan University, 2020 Spring, *Chapter V Surfaces* homework, downloaded to `tmp/sources/ntu-ag2-chapter5.pdf`: Exercise 1 of §3 (PDF p. 9) attempts V.3.1 for a centre of any codimension: its formal-functions reduction is right, but the induction that follows uses $H^i(\PP^{r-1},\OO(n))=0$, the cohomology of a fibre, which is the cohomology of $E$ only when the centre is a point; Exercise 4 of §3 (PDF pp. 10--11) proves all of V.3.4, with the length computation $\length(A/\mathfrak m^n)-\length(A/\mathfrak m^{n-r})=nr-\frac{r(r-1)}2$ for (d) and the cone for (e); Exercise 5 of §3 (PDF p. 11), in characteristic not $2$, gets $\delta_P=\frac12(r-2)(r-3)+\lfloor(r-2)/2\rfloor$ and $g=\lfloor(r-1)/2\rfloor$ for V.3.5; Exercise 7 of §3 (PDF pp. 12--13) blows each germ of V.3.7 up until its strict transform is nonsingular --- twice for (a), (b), (d) and (e), once for (c) --- and stops there, drawing the incidence graph of the curves produced and never blowing up at smooth points to make the total transform normal crossings, so it settles $\delta=4,4,3,4,4$ and the classification (a),(b),(d) equivalent, (c) and (e) separate, and not the embedded resolution; Exercise 8 of §3 (PDF pp. 13--14, its (a) on p. 13 and its (b) on p. 14) gets $\delta=7$ and $9$ for V.3.8, which refutes the printed claim, and then guesses a different equation for (b). Yang Pi-Yeh, *Hartshorne Solutions* (`tmp/sources/lfwin-hartshorne-solutions.pdf`, 2019): V.3.1 at printed p. 107 assumes codimension one and is not a proof of the exercise; V.3.4 at printed pp. 107--108 identifies $\mathrm{gr}_{\mathfrak m}A$ with a polynomial ring in (b) and gives a wrong length formula in (d); V.3.5 at printed p. 108 takes $\delta=(r-2)(r-3)/2$, omitting the residual singularity; V.3.7 at printed p. 108 writes the successive strict transforms, including the further blowup at a smooth point that produces the normal crossings, and closes "So $(a),(b),(d)$ are equivalent to each other. And $(c),(e)$ are not equivalent to any others" --- so he does decide the equivalence, and what he does not do is compute $\delta$; V.3.8 at printed pp. 108--109, its (a) on p. 108 and its (b) on p. 109, asserts without computing that the two $\delta$'s are the same, which is false, and that the curves are not equivalent. V.3.6 has the forward implication at printed p. 108 by a completion argument and asserts the counterexample; its published Puiseux criterion is Wall, *Singular Points of Plane Curves*, Ch. 3, which is not available here and is cited as printed.

**State after the transcription pass of 2026-11-16.** Three of the six are closed on published proofs, transcribed onto their cards with the page. V.3.4(d),(e) on NTU Exercise 4 of §3, PDF pp. 10--11: step `curve-length-formula` is its exact sequence $0\to R/\mfm^{l-r}\to R/\mfm^l\to B/\mfm_C^l\to0$ and its length computation $nr-\frac12r(r-1)$, and the order-additivity sentence the source leaves out is supplied on the step; its display names the two maps of that sequence the wrong way round, which the step records. **Corrected for V.3.5 (2026-11-16).** The paragraph after the statement had said that a hyperelliptic curve needs a *separable* degree-two morphism and that $\PP^1$ has none; both claims are false, since $\PP^1$ carries the separable degree-two maps $z\mapsto z^2$ away from characteristic $2$ and $z\mapsto z^2+z$ in characteristic $2$, whose derivative $2z+1$ is the constant $1$, and Hartshorne IV, Ex. 1.7, printed p. 298, asks only for genus at least $2$ and a finite morphism of degree $2$. The paragraph now gives the reason that holds, that in characteristic $2$ the field $k(Y)=k(\sqrt{x-a_1})$ is rational, so the normalization is $\PP^1$ of genus $0$ and no curve of the construction meets the printed definition. Step `delta-invariant-formula` had said that the terminal germ for $e=0$ meets no point; the strict transform meets the last exceptional curve in the two points $x=1$ and $x=-1$, and both statements are corrected on the card, whose audit note of 2026-11-11 keeps the withdrawn wording as the record of that pass.

### V.4.3 and V.4.4(b) of `SRC-TEXT-HART77` have no complete published solution

**Object and need.** Two requests in `SRC-TEXT-HART77` §V.4 are proved on their cards without a published argument to check them against: `P-AGH543ORDINARYSING` (V.4.3, printed p. 407, quadratic transformations producing only ordinary singularities) and `P-AGH544CUBICGROUPLAW` in its part (b) (V.4.4(b), printed p. 407, associativity of the chord-and-tangent law).

**Observed evidence.** Andrew Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (October 3, 2013), PDF pp. 285--296 for §V.4, is again the only retained set that reaches the section. V.4.3 is the whole line "See Algebraic Curves over Finite Fields by Hirschfeld, Theorem 3.27", and Hirschfeld's book is not among the retained files. V.4.4(a) he proves by Cayley--Bacharach on $PP'\cup QQ'\cup RR'$ and $L\cup L'\cup P''Q''$, but V.4.4(b) is "See Tate, Silverman: Rational Points. It's in the first chapter. They even give nice pictures", with no argument. His V.4.1 states $\pi\circ\psi=\mathrm{id}_{\PP^2}$ and $\psi\circ\pi=\mathrm{id}_Q$, which are false as written, though the identification it is used for is right.

**Impact and owner.** V.4.4(b) keeps a complete proof, and V.4.3 has one only over a field of characteristic $0$. Over such a field V.4.3 replaces the resolution blowups of (3.8) by quadratic transformations with two auxiliary centres chosen so that the joining lines meet $C$ at the bad point with exactly $\mu_P(C)$ and elsewhere transversely; the three contracted fundamental lines then give ordinary multiple points and every other germ is carried isomorphically, and the projection is separable so the auxiliary lines exist. In positive characteristic the projection from a bad point can be inseparable and the step that chooses the two auxiliary lines fails there; the card takes that case from Hirschfeld's Theorem 3.27, a book that is not in `tmp/sources` and was not read, and it now says on the step that this case is a citation and not a proof. **So the V.4.3 obligation is not met by the card's own proof**, which covers characteristic $0$ alone. V.4.4(b) is derived from part (a) by the configuration $A=P*Q$, $B=Q*R$, $V=P*T$, where part (a) applied to the triples $(P,Q,A)$ and $(T,B,P_0)$ gives $V,R,S$ collinear, so that $(P+Q)+R=\iota(V)=P+(Q+R)$.

**Uncertainty.** Searched: all twelve retained Hartshorne solution files in `tmp/sources` by `pdftotext -layout` extraction, plus `assets/attachments/Hartshorne_Solutions.pdf` (the Cais notes). Chapter V occurs only in Egbert (V.1--V.6) and in Park (§V.5 alone). Conclusion: no complete published solution for the two requests above. Confidence: high for these sets. Gaps: a published treatment may exist outside them.

**Located sources.** Two solution sets outside the twelve previously inspected reach these exercises. Algebraic Geometry II, National Taiwan University, 2020 Spring, *Chapter V Surfaces* homework, downloaded to `tmp/sources/ntu-ag2-chapter5.pdf`: Exercise 4(b) of §4 (Tzu-Yang Chou), PDF p. 16, proves associativity by the configuration $PQ\cap C=P,Q,R$, $P_0R\cap C=T$, $TU\cap C=V$, $P_0V\cap C=W$, $QU\cap C=X$, $PV\cap C=Y$, part (a) giving $P_0,X,Y$ collinear and so $(P+Q)+U=T+U=W=P+Y=P+(Q+U)$ — a complete published proof of V.4.4(b) — and Exercise 3 of §4 (Shuang-Yen Lee), PDF pp. 15--16, attempts V.4.3 with two auxiliary centres through the bad point and a chart analysis of the multiplicity at its image, but never shows that the three contracted points are ordinary, so V.4.3 still has no complete published proof. Yang Pi-Yeh, *Hartshorne Solutions* (`tmp/sources/lfwin-hartshorne-solutions.pdf`, 2019), gives V.4.4(b) at printed p. 109 by a different configuration with the same shape, and V.4.3 at printed p. 109 as a termination argument with the ordinary-ness of the contracted points asserted. Hirschfeld, *Algebraic Curves over Finite Fields*, Theorem 3.27, cited by Egbert, remains unconsulted; the cards for V.4.3 now state that the inseparable projection case is the one taken from that theorem.
