## 2026-11-16: a reader's report on the V.4.15 count and the V.4.16 count of five — the passage through Dolgachev's generators carried, and the count of five derived from the criteria

**Object and need.** The two cards `P-AGH5415GENPOSITION` (V.4.15) and `P-AGH5416FERMATCUBIC` (V.4.16), and the record of this date headed "a reader's report on the four V-batch cards of #121 --- the round's records restored to the text they were introduced with, V.4.15(c) and V.4.16's incidence relations restored as the cards' own, and two statements of V.4.15's count corrected", whose V.4.15 item (ii) makes one of the findings below. A local reader read the repair round against the sources and the book and did not accept it; the two findings it left are repaired here. The record of this date is left as written (`QUAL-11`), and what it gets wrong is stated here.

**V.4.15: the claim that no source prints the generation is false.** The step `count-fifty-six-and-two-forty` said that joining Dolgachev's $W(\mathbf E_N)$-orbit to Nagata's similarity classes through Lemma 2.4, printed p. 279, "also needs $W(\mathbf E_N)$ to be generated by the permutations together with $r_{\alpha_{123}}$, which no source read for this card prints", and so did not carry the passage; the record above says the same. Dolgachev's *Topics*, a source of this card, prints it. Theorem 8.2.11, printed p. 258, is the statement that $W(\mathbf E_N)$ is the subgroup of $\mathbf O(\mathbf E_N)$ generated by the reflections $r_{\beta_i}$ in a canonical root basis $\beta$; the canonical basis (8.5), printed p. 257, is $\beta_1=\alpha_{123}$ and $\beta_i=\alpha_{i-1,i}$ for $i\ge2$; and the sentence after Definition 7.5, printed p. 235, says that the subgroup generated by the reflections $r_{\alpha_i}$, $i\ne0$, acts as the permutation group $\mathfrak S_N$ of $\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_N$. On a vector $v=d\mathbf e_0-\sum_im_i\mathbf e_i$, the reflection in $\alpha_{123}=\mathbf e_0-\mathbf e_1-\mathbf e_2-\mathbf e_3$ has $(v,\alpha_{123})=d-m_1-m_2-m_3=a$ and sends $v$ to $(d+a)\mathbf e_0-(m_1+a)\mathbf e_1-(m_2+a)\mathbf e_2-(m_3+a)\mathbf e_3-\sum_{i\ge4}m_i\mathbf e_i$, which is Nagata's operator $\mathfrak q$ of Section 2, printed p. 279; with Lemma 2.4, which makes similarity the relation generated by $\mathfrak q$ and the permutations of the multiplicities, the similarity classes are therefore the $W(\mathbf E_N)$-orbits, and the solutions of $\mathbf k_N\cdot v=-1$ and $v^2=-1$ are one such orbit, the one containing the degree-$1$ family $\mathbf e_0-\mathbf e_i-\mathbf e_j$ that Proposition 8.2.15 lists, that is, the pre-exceptional class. The step now carries that passage at those printed pages, and the count $240$ does not depend on it: it rests on Nagata's table on printed p. 284 and Dolgachev's table on printed p. 261, as before.

**V.4.15: what the paper prints as the pre-exceptional type.** Reading printed p. 280 of Nagata as an image rendered at 200 dpi from `tmp/sources/nagata-1960-rational-surfaces-ii.pdf` (PDF 10, whose folio is 280) gives "Elements of $\mathfrak E(1,1,1,0,\ldots,0)$ (with $r-2$ zeros)", three $1$s with $r-2$ zeros, which is $r+1$ entries in an $r$-tuple; Proposition 3 on printed p. 279, read the same way, prints the same extra $1$ in "$(1,1,1,1,0,\ldots,0)$ (with $r-3$ zeros)" for the class of a line through three of the points. The class the notion needs is the class of a line through two of them, $(1,1,0,\ldots,0)$ with $r-2$ zeros, which is the representative the proof of Theorem 2a carries by $\mathfrak q$ to $\mathcal L(0;-P_1)$, and it is the only one of the two that satisfies the two equations $d^2-\sum_im_i^2=-1$ and $3d-\sum_im_i=1$ the same proof writes. The card had copied the printed form and so contradicted its own invariants; the solution's bullet now states the class of a line through two of the points and names what the paper prints, the source's printing being named on the card rather than copied or patched.

**V.4.16: the count of five now derived from the criteria.** The step `two-skew-lines-meet-five` stated Gathmann's Corollary 11.2(b) and said that his proof is the sentence "The proof of part (b) is analogous", printed p. 91, and that no check was carried out on the card, so the count of five stood on no argument; the card's own pair-by-pair criteria, restored in this batch, decide every pair, and the count follows from them. The step now carries that derivation, marked as the card's own, and sits after `incidence-count-ten-sixteen` so that every step it cites comes before it. The derivation runs the two positions a skew pair can occupy. Two lines in one family, $A_{ab}$ and $A_{cd}$ with $a\ne c$ and $b\ne d$, are met by the two lines $A_{ad}$ and $A_{cb}$ of that family; a $B$-line meets both exactly when $a'-b'\equiv a-b\equiv c-d$ and a $C$-line exactly when $a'+b'\equiv a+b\equiv c+d$, and with $x=a-c$ and $y=b-d$ both nonzero these two conditions are $x\equiv y$ and $x\equiv-y$, so exactly one holds and gives three more lines. Two lines in different families reduce, by the transposition of $x_1$ and $x_2$, which preserves $S$, interchanges the $A$- and $B$-families and maps $C_{ab}$ to $C_{ba}$, to $A_{ab}$ and $B_{cd}$ with $a+d\not\equiv b+c$, which two $A$-lines, two $B$-lines and one $C$-line meet. The count was also checked exhaustively over $\mathrm{GF}(7)$, where $2$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $3$ is invertible: the $27$ lines are distinct, each meets exactly $10$ of the others, all four criteria hold for all $27\times27$ pairs, and each of the $216$ skew pairs, $54$ within one family and $162$ across two, has exactly $5$ common transversals. That check is a confirmation of the derivation and not evidence replacing it.

**Repair.** `P-AGH5415GENPOSITION` in `1e8496cfb9`; `P-AGH5416FERMATCUBIC` in `98523c3f07`; this record in the COMPLAINTS commit that carries it, which changes no card. ## 2026-11-16: three statements of the #123 Hatcher record of this date are false and are withdrawn

**Object and need.** The record of this date introduced by `a1847addac` — "the #123 Hatcher record restored to its introduced text, and the cube argument's completion corrected" — and the `E-HAT-4.1-7` audit event of this date added by `a7dffb24e6`. The rendered card and the restored Hatcher record are read and accepted. Three statements inside this round's own text are false, and they are withdrawn here, each named, with no replacement argument: the card uses none of that text, and proves the independence of the chosen extension from May.

**(1) The dimension.** "the whole of $T$, now prescribed, is the $J$-configuration of the $(n+1)$-cube in $I^{n+2}$" is wrong in its dimension. $T$ lies in $I^n\times I\times I=I^{n+2}$, and the $J$-configuration of the sentence is that of the $(n+2)$-cube; the $(n+1)$-cube is the piece $I^{n-1}\times I\times I$ of the first step.

**(2) The reason $\hat\psi$ lands in $A$.** "$\hat\psi$ because $J^{n-1}$ is pinned at $v(t)$" is false as stated. On $J^{n-1}\times I\times I$ the value of $\hat\psi$ is $\psi(t,u)$, the value of the path homotopy $\psi:v\simeq w$, and that equals $v(t)$ only at $u=0$.

**(3) Which earlier passes said it.** "An extension into $A$ is therefore needed, which is what the passes before this round said" is half true. The `source-corrected` event of this date that `b5e7fe9edb` added to the card said it — "an extension over a J-type subset of a cube into $A$ ... exists by the same retraction" — and the event that `9c80ec98b1` added after it said the opposite: "an arbitrary subspace $A$ has no such extension property", and "no extension into $A$ is used".

## 2026-11-16: V.6.2's equality case is open in the sources read, and items (i) and (iv) of this date's earlier V.6.2 report are withdrawn

**Object and need, 2026-11-16.** The card `P-AGH562CHERNGRIFFITHS` (Hartshorne V.6.2) and the V.6.2 items of this date's record headed "a reader's third report on the four §V.5--§V.6 cards of #121 -- the markings moved into the steps, and three attributions corrected". A local reader read the fourth round against the two entries and the book and did not accept the card. All five of its findings are right. Two of them bear on that record, whose items (i) and (iv) contradict each other; both are withdrawn here, in this record, and neither is edited in place. The card carries its five repairs in the `source-corrected` event of this date that `799a22819f` added.

**The equality case, 2026-11-16: no published derivation was located, and the case is open.** Let $X\subset\PP^{n+1}$ have $d=2n$, and let $L=\OO_C(1)$ be special. Yang Pi-Yeh, solution 5.6.2, printed p. 115, prints "$2g-2=d+H\cdot K\ge d$" from adjunction and "$n+1\le h^0(\OO_H(d))=1-g+d$", and concludes "Then $2n+2\le2-2g+2d\le d$, so here we must have $d=2g-2$, i.e. $d=2n$ and $g=n+1$, and $H\cdot K=0$". At $d=2n$ those two printed inequalities read $g\le n$ and $g\ge n+1$, so the chain is contradictory: it refutes the non-special case, the case it was eliminating, and yields no $d=2g-2$. The "$=1-g+d$" is the value Riemann--Roch gives $h^0$ when $h^1=0$, and in the equality case $h^1(C,L)\ne0$: if $L\cong\omega_C$ then $d=2g-2$, $h^1(C,L)=h^0(C,\OO_C)=1$ and $h^0(C,L)=g=1-g+d+1$. His "so here we must have $d=2g-2$" is a non sequitur, and the card no longer reports it as a derivation. Egbert, V.6.2, printed p. 303, takes a nonzero effective $D\sim rK_X$, which Theorem 6.1 gives for $X$ not ruled, reads $2g-2=d+\frac1rH\cdot D\ge d$ off adjunction, which excludes the non-special case only, and then writes "Then $d=2n$, $g=n+1$ so $d=2(g-1)=2g-2$" with no argument --- the skipped Clifford-equality step --- and gets $H\cdot K=0$ from the genus formula $n+1=p_a(H)=1+\frac12(2n+HK)$. So neither entry derives $d=2g-2$ in this case, and no published proof of the equality case of Clifford's theorem for V.6.2 is in the sources read. The case is open under [#121](https://github.com/dzackgarza/new-qual-site/issues/121). The card keeps its own proof of it, in steps `clifford-equality-canonical` and `canonical-meets-hyperplane-zero`, and both steps say that it is the card's own; what the two entries write and take is stated as they write and take it, and the remark no longer says the case is published twice.

**Withdrawn, 2026-11-16: items (i) and (iv) of that record.** Item (i) said "Yang gets it from $2g-2=d+H\cdot K_X\ge d$ with Clifford's bound $n+1\le h^0(C,L)$ and $2n+2\le2-2g+2d\le d$, and Egbert from a nonzero effective $D\sim rK_X$ for $X$ not ruled, which gives $2g-2=d+(1/r)H\cdot D\ge d$": neither of those is a derivation of $d=2g-2$, for the reasons above, and item (iv)'s closing clause --- that Yang's $n+1\le h^0(\OO_H(d))=1-g+d$ "is the non-special hypothesis of his chain, which the chain refutes" --- says so and contradicts it. That clause is right; what does not stand with it is item (iv)'s own conclusion, that the non-special case "is published" in a form the card may attribute. What Yang prints there is the identity $h^2(X,\OO_X)=h^1(C,\OO_C(1))$, which his entry does not prove and which asserts that the restriction map $H^0(X,\omega_X)\to H^0(C,\omega_X\restriction_C)$ is an isomorphism, which it need not be: its kernel is $H^0(X,\omega_X(-C))$ and its cokernel sits in $H^1(X,\omega_X(-C))$, neither of which vanishes in general. Egbert's dichotomy, for its part, is special against non-special for $\OO_H(d)$ itself, with no relation of $p_g(X)$ to $h^1(C,L)$. So (i) and (iv) are withdrawn whole, and what stands instead is on the card: step `nonspecial-implies-pg-zero` states each entry's route as printed, and the card's own proof of the implication that step states is marked as its own.

**Theorem number, 2026-11-16: the criterion used is Theorem 6.1, not 6.2.** The card cited "Theorem 6.2, printed p. 422" for the nonemptiness of the linear system of $12K$ on a surface that is not ruled. Read in `tmp/sources/hartshorne-1977-algebraic-geometry.md`, printed p. 422 (PDF p. 437, printed $=$ PDF $-15$) carries "Theorem 6.1. $\kappa=-1\Leftrightarrow$ the linear system of $12K$ is empty $\Leftrightarrow X$ is either rational or ruled" and "Theorem 6.2 (Castelnuovo). $X$ is rational $\Leftrightarrow p_a=P_2=0$". Both entries cite the book's 6.1 as "theorem 6.2" --- Yang's "Then by theorem 6.2", Egbert's "by thm 6.2" --- and the card had repeated their number as the book's; a remark of `0d013c480b` had recorded the miscitation, and the rewrite of `0637efe130` dropped it. The step now cites Theorem 6.1, and the remark says what each entry numbers.

**The closing chain and Exercise V.1.1, 2026-11-16.** The card had the two entries' closing as "Kodaira vanishing gives $H^1(X,\OO_X(A))=H^1(X,\OO_X(K_X+A))=0$, and Serre duality gives $H^1(X,\OO_X(K_X-A))=0$", with $A-K_X\sim A$ ample. That swaps the two theorems and uses $K_X$ trivial, which neither entry has at that point. Both take $H-K_X$ ample by Nakai--Moishezon; Kodaira vanishing on that ample class gives $H^1(X,\OO_X(H))=0$, since $\omega_X\otimes\OO_X(H-K_X)\cong\OO_X(H)$, and Serre duality gives $H^1(X,\OO_X(K_X-H))=0$. The entries print the two vanishings in the opposite order, naming Kodaira vanishing for $H^1(X,\OO_X(K_X-H))$ and Serre duality for $H^1(X,\OO_X(H))$, and the card now states them that way. Both also cite Exercise V.1.1 for $H^0(X,\OO_X(K_X-H))=0$; the book's Exercise V.1.1, printed p. 366, is the identity $C\cdot D=\chi(\OO_X)-\chi(\mathcal L^{-1})-\chi(\mathcal M^{-1})+\chi(\mathcal L^{-1}\otimes\mathcal M^{-1})$ and states no such vanishing. It follows instead because $(K_X-H)\cdot H=-d<0$ with $H$ ample, and the card now gives that reason and records their citation.

## 2026-11-16: a reader's report on the II.3.10(b) records of this date and on five cards of #121 --- the kernel is Cais's, the counterexample is false, and the text-version paths leave the rendered cards

**The kernel, 2026-11-16: `ker psi = pB` is Cais's own slip of notation, and the card now names it as his.** The record of this date beginning "Correction, 2026-11-16, on the reader's report of #121: the two letters and the kernel in the transcription of Cais's 3.10(a)" ends by saying that both errors are the card's transcription and not Cais's, "whose own letters are consistent throughout, so nothing is named as his defect". That is true of the letters and false of the kernel. Cais writes, at line 283 of `tmp/sources/hartshorne-solutions-cais.md`, "Since ker $\psi = pB$": his $B$ is the total ring and $p$ the base prime, so that $pB$ is an ideal of the total ring, while $\psi$ has $B\otimes_AA_p$ as its source and $\ker\psi$ is an ideal of that ring. The card's earlier $\ker\psi=\mfp A$ was therefore his imprecision transcribed faithfully, and the kernel error is his. The card's step `uy-homeomorphism-onto-fiber` now says so: it states the kernel as $\mfp(A\otimes_BB_\mfp)$, records that his $pB$ is an ideal of the total space and the identity his slip of notation, and proves the prime-level form his argument uses, that a prime $\mfq$ of the total space contains $pB$ exactly when $g^{-1}(\mfq)=\mfp$. The card's event of this date whose note begins "Repair on the reader's report, on two letters and one kernel" quotes his line and is left as written; the event appended after it, in `4dc200e625`, records the naming. The record above is left as written, and nothing else in that entry changes.

**The counterexample, 2026-11-16: the example in this date's record on the contraction of the kernel is false, and the example that shows the gap needs $S$-torsion.** The record beginning "Correction, 2026-11-16, on the record above of this date: the contraction of the kernel is not $\mfp A$" takes $B=k[s]$, $\mfp=(s)$ and $A=B[x]$, and says that $A\otimes_BB_\mfp$ is $A_s$, in which $s$ is a unit, so that $\mfp(A_s)=A_s$ has contraction $A$ while $\mfp A=sA$ is proper. It fails at the first step: $s$ lies in $\mfp$, so $s\notin S=k[s]-\mfp$, and $s$ is not a unit of $B_\mfp=k[s]_{(s)}$. The tensor is $B_\mfp[x]=k[s]_{(s)}[x]$, in which $\mfp$ generates the proper ideal $(s)$ whose contraction to $A$ is $sA=\mfp A$; that example exhibits no gap at all. What the contraction is: it is $\set{a\in A \st sa\in\mfp A \text{ for some } s\in S}$, the $S$-saturation of $\mfp A$ in $A$, so it is strictly larger than $\mfp A$ exactly when some $s\in S$ is a zero divisor on $A/\mfp A$. One ring where that happens: $B=k[s,t]$, $\mfp=(s)$ and $A=k[s,t,x]/(tx-s)$. There $t\in S$ and $t\cdot x=s\in\mfp A=(s)$, while $x\notin(s)$, the quotient $A/(s)$ being $k[t,x]$; so the contraction contains $x$ and is strictly larger than $\mfp A$. The prime-level statement the record above keeps is unaffected, and it is the one the card states: a prime $\mfq\subseteq A$ with $\mfq\cap S=\emptyset$ contains the contraction exactly when it contains $\mfp A$, because no element of $S$ lies in $\mfq$. The record above is left as written, this record is its correction, and no text on the card changes with it.

**III.7.4(b),(d), 2026-11-16: the parts are the card's own, and that is all the reading establishes.** The head of the solution on `P-AGH374COHOMCLASS` said that (b) and (d) "have no published proof", and the second paragraph of its published-solution remark that they "are not published". Both say more than the evidence: what this file's III.7.4(b),(d) entry records and what the fifth and sixth passes on the card recorded is that no published proof was found in the sources read and searched, which is not that none exists. The two sentences now mark the parts as the card's own and stop there; the descriptions they open --- Yang's (b) with its citation to his own 3.7.3, his (d) in homogeneous coordinates by Euler's formula, Kim's fragment of (b) and no (d), and the class-level halves of the Stacks tags with no comparison with the trace of III.7 --- stand as written, and so do the closing sentences saying that steps `s2`, `s3`, `s5` and `s6` prove both parts relative to the inputs (R) and (B). No step, page or tag moves.

**The text versions, 2026-11-16: eight rendered passages on five cards of #121 named files in `tmp/sources`.** The solution head of `P-AGH2310FIBRES`; the head and the published-solution remark of `P-AGH2320DIMENSION`; the head and the remark of `P-AGH3117NONALGSHEAF`; the remark of `P-AGH3123JUMPINGIDEAL`, at two places; and the proof of (a) at the head of step `s1` and the published-solution remark of `P-AGH374COHOMCLASS`. **The hypothesis, 2026-11-16: the prime-level form of Cais's kernel statement needs the prime to meet $g(B-\mfp)$ trivially.** The record above of this date states it as "a prime $\mfq$ of the total space contains $pB$ exactly when $g^{-1}(\mfq)=\mfp$", and that is false without the hypothesis: for $g$ the identity of $k[s,t]$ and $\mfp=(s)$, the prime $(s,t)$ contains $pB=(s)$ and contracts to $(s,t)$ and not to $\mfp$. ## 2026-11-16: a reader's fourth report on the two V.4.15 and V.4.16 repairs — the pre-exceptional type is not misprinted, and the two-family reduction was made by the wrong transposition

**Object and need.** The record of this date headed "a reader's report on the V.4.15 count and the V.4.16 count of five --- the passage through Dolgachev's generators carried, and the count of five derived from the criteria", and the two cards it repaired, `P-AGH5415GENPOSITION` (V.4.15) and `P-AGH5416FERMATCUBIC` (V.4.16). A local reader read that round against the sources and the book and did not accept two of its changes, both of them defects that round introduced. The record of this date is left as written (`QUAL-11`), and what it gets wrong is stated here; each card carries the correction in an event of this date appended today.

**V.4.15: Nagata does not misprint the pre-exceptional type, and the replacement was not a type.** The record above says that printed p. 280 prints "Elements of $\mathfrak E(1,1,1,0,\ldots,0)$ (with $r-2$ zeros)", "three $1$s with $r-2$ zeros, which is $r+1$ entries in an $r$-tuple", and that the card's bullet was therefore changed to $(1,1,0,\ldots,0)$ with $r-2$ zeros, the printed form being named a misprint. That is wrong twice. A numerical type is $(d,m_1,\ldots,m_r)$, so it has $r+1$ entries and not $r$: three $1$s followed by $r-2$ zeros are exactly $d=1$, $m_1=m_2=1$ and $m_3=\cdots=m_r=0$, the class of a line through two of the points, and that type satisfies $d^2-\sum_im_i^2=1-2=-1$ and $3d-\sum_im_i=3-2=1$, the two equations the same record says the printed representative does not satisfy. The replacement, $(1,1,0,\ldots,0)$ with $r-2$ zeros, has $r$ entries and is not a numerical type with $r$ base points at all. Proposition 3's $(1,1,1,1,0,\ldots,0)$ "with $r-3$ zeros", printed p. 279, is $d=1$ with three points, likewise $r+1$ entries, so neither place misprints anything and there is no source defect to name. Both cards of the printed pages had been rendered at 200 dpi and read correctly; the arithmetic of the entry count was the round's own error, not the paper's. The bullet again prints the representative as the paper does and unpacks it as $d=1$, $m_1=m_2=1$, $m_3=\cdots=m_r=0$, and the step's sentence on the degree-$1$ family says the same.

**V.4.16: the reduction of the two-family case used a transposition that does not perform it.** The record above says that the transposition of $x_1$ and $x_2$ "preserves $S$, interchanges the $A$- and $B$-families and maps $C_{ab}$ to $C_{ba}$", and on that ground reduced every two-family skew pair to the form $A_{ab}$, $B_{cd}$; the step said the same. The transposition does interchange $A$ and $B$, which the count of $5$ for that pairing needs, but it keeps the $C$-family and sends $C_{ab}$ to $C_{a,-b}$, so it carries an $A$--$C$ pair to a $B$--$C$ pair and a $B$--$C$ pair to an $A$--$C$ pair, and reaches the $A$--$B$ form from neither; the count of five for those two pairings was therefore not derived. The transpositions that do the reduction are the other two: $x_2$ with $x_3$ keeps the $A$-family, sending $A_{ab}$ to $A_{a,-b}$, and interchanges $B$ and $C$, sending $B_{ab}$ to $C_{ab}$ and $C_{ab}$ to $B_{ab}$, so it carries an $A$--$C$ pair to an $A$--$B$ pair; and $x_1$ with $x_3$ keeps the $B$-family, sending $B_{ab}$ to $B_{a,-b}$, and interchanges $A$ and $C$, so it carries a $B$--$C$ pair to an $A$--$B$ pair. The step now names those two and states what makes the relabelling legitimate, that a projectivity maps the twenty-seven lines to themselves and preserves incidences, so a pair and its image have equally many common transversals. The exhaustive computation over $\mathrm{GF}(7)$ recorded above was a confirmation of the whole count and not a derivation; the family actions it was used to suggest were checked again here and are the three stated, and the count of $5$ for each of the $162$ skew pairs across families is what the corrected reduction derives.

## 2026-11-16: a reader's whole-card reading of the IV.3.11 card --- Harris's lower bound is the cones over the surface, not over the secant variety

**The object, 2026-11-16: the cones in Harris's lower bound have base $X$, and the card's remark and one record of this date give them base $S(X)$.** Harris, Example 11.22, printed p. 144, in the paragraph of the Veronese surface (text version `tmp/sources/harris-1992-algebraic-geometry-first-course-pp128-149.md`, line 352), writes "since it is clear on elementary grounds that $S(X)$ cannot have dimension less than $4$ (for example, the cones $\overline{p,S}$ over $S$ with vertex a point $p\in S$ would all have to coincide)". The letters are ambiguous as printed. Read with $S=S(X)$ the argument does not run: nothing on the card or in Harris puts the cone over $S(X)$ with a vertex on it inside $S(X)$. Read with $S=X$, it does: for $p\in X$ every line joining $p$ to a point of $X$ is a secant line, so the cone $\overline{p,X}$ lies in $S(X)$, and it is three-dimensional, being the union of a surface's worth of lines through $p$; were $\dim S(X)$ equal to $3$, each such cone would be $S(X)$, and cones with different vertices do not coincide. The card's published-solution remark said "the cones over $S(X)$ with vertex a point of it", which is the reading that fails, and the audit event of `ba3057319b` says the same; the remark now carries the cones over $X$ with the containment that makes the argument run, and a new event of this date records the correction. Harris's sentence is quoted unchanged at step `secant-dim-lower`, inside quotation marks and as his words. ## 2026-11-16: a correction to this date's record of Harris's lower bound --- the contradiction is the span of $X$, not the distinctness of the vertices

**The false clause, 2026-11-16: "cones with different vertices do not coincide" is not a general truth, and the contradiction is drawn from the span.** The record of this date headed "a reader's whole-card reading of the IV.3.11 card --- Harris's lower bound is the cones over the surface, not over the secant variety" argues the bound with "were $\dim S(X)$ equal to $3$, each such cone would be $S(X)$, and cones with different vertices do not coincide". The last clause is false as stated: a linear subspace is a cone with vertex at each of its points, so two cones with different vertices may well coincide. The contradiction Harris's sentence gestures at is real, but it comes from elsewhere. Suppose $\dim S(X)=3$. Then for every $p\in X$ the cone $\overline{p,X}$, being three-dimensional and contained in $S(X)$, equals $S(X)$; so $S(X)$ is the union of the lines $\overline{pq}$ with $q\in X$, for each $p\in X$ separately. Hence, for $p\in X$ and $x\in S(X)$, the point $x$ lies on one of those lines and the line $\overline{px}$ is contained in $S(X)$; and then, whenever a linear subspace $\Lambda\subseteq S(X)$ and a point $p\in X$ are given, the span $\langle\Lambda,p\rangle$ is contained in $S(X)$, being the union of the lines $\overline{py}$ over $y\in\Lambda$ (or $\Lambda$ itself when $p\in\Lambda$). Starting from a point $p_0\in X$ and adjoining points $p_1,\dots,p_k$ of $X$ one at a time, $\langle p_0,\dots,p_k\rangle\subseteq S(X)$ at every step, so with $k$ large enough that $p_0,\dots,p_k$ span $X$ the whole of $\PP^5=\langle X\rangle$ lies in $S(X)$, against $\dim S(X)=3$. The contradiction is the nondegeneracy of $X$ in $\PP^5$, which the exercise's own statement uses, and not any distinctness of vertices. The record above stands as written, being a record of its day, and its clause is corrected here.

**The card, 2026-11-16: nothing on it asserts the false clause.** The published-solution remark and the audit event of this date stop at "would all have to coincide", which is Harris's own phrasing of the lower bound and states nothing false; Harris's sentence is quoted verbatim at step `secant-dim-lower`. No card text changes in this pass.

**Repair, 2026-11-16:** this record in the COMPLAINTS commit that carries it, which changes no card. No dated event and no earlier record is edited in place, this record and the one it corrects included.

**Uncertainty, 2026-11-16: what was read for this record, and what was not.** Read: the record of this date it corrects, the card's published-solution remark and its audit event, Harris's sentence at printed p. 144 of Example 11.22 as already read in `tmp/sources/harris-1992-algebraic-geometry-first-course-pp128-149.md` at line 352, and the exercise's statement, which has $X$ spanning $\PP^5$ as a surface in $\PP^5$. Not read: the printed book itself, and no source was read again for this record; the argument above is checked on the page, not taken from any secondary account.

## 2026-11-17: IV.1.10's singular case is published — KReiser's two-case argument for the point's regularity, and the gap named in the printed NTU solution

**The obligation, 2026-11-17: the record that has held this card open since 2026-11-15 is discharged by a published argument rather than by the card's own.** The entry "IV.1–IV.3 — the parts whose retained entries assert the decisive step" lists `P-AGH4110PICOFARITHGENUSONE` (IV.1.10, printed p. 299) among six cards whose retained entries assert the decisive step, and its Impact paragraph says that IV.1.10 is proved "by the exact sequence with $\OO_Z(E)$ and the principal-maximal-ideal criterion for regularity", that is by the card. #121 asks instead for a complete published solution cited on the card, and the singular case is where the two retained entries stopped: Egbert closes at $\dim\abs{D+P_0}=0$ and Cais asserts that the point is "necessarily in $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ as $D$ is supported in $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$" without arguing it (quoted in that entry). Two sources supplied for this date now cover the singular case between them, and the card's step `s6` cites both.

**What the printed NTU solution proves, 2026-11-17, and where it stops.** Exercise 10 of §1 of *Algebraic Geometry II*, National Taiwan University, 2020 Spring (course of Chin-Lung Wang), Chapter IV, by Ping-Hsun Chuang, printed pp. 3--4 of `tmp/sources/ntu-ag2-chapter4.pdf`, text version `tmp/sources/ntu-ag2-chapter4.md`: the heading closes printed p. 3 and the proof stands on printed p. 4, the folio being the PDF page number, as the chapter V set of the same series has it. It applies Exercise IV.1.9 to $D=K$, uses $h^0(X,\omega_X^\circ)=h^1(X,\OO_X)=p_a$ through Serre duality for a locally complete intersection, gets $\deg K=p_a-1=0$, applies IV.1.9 again to $D+P_0$, has $\deg(K-D-P_0)=-1$ and hence $\ell(K-D-P_0)=0$, and concludes $\ell(D+P_0)=1$: "there exists a unique $R>0$ such that $R\sim D+P_0$. Therefore, for any $D\in\Pic^0X$, we find a unique $R$ such that $D\sim R-P_0$ and thus $X_{\mathrm{reg}}\to\Pic^0X$ is bijection." The last sentence is the exercise's conclusion and is not argued: nothing in it shows that the point supporting $R$ is a regular point of $X$, which is exactly what Hartshorne's $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ asks and what the exercise's published entries leave open. The MinerU text version loses the arrow of that last display, printing "X_reg Pic^0 X is bijection" where printed p. 4 has "Xreg → Pic0 X"; the proof was read on the page for that sentence.

**What fills it, 2026-11-17: KReiser's accepted answer 4978046 to Math Stack Exchange question 4962032, which asks for this step alone.** The answer, posted 2024-09-29 to a question asked by François Gatine on 2024-08-23 and accepted there, takes a non-regular point $Q$ and $\mcl\cong\OO_X(Q-P_0)$ and normalizes: with two or more points above $Q$ a function vanishing at $Q$ vanishes at each of them, so $\nu^*\OO_X(Q-P_0)$ has positive degree; with one point $\widetilde Q$ above $Q$, Hartshorne's Lemma II.7.4 (printed p. 153, PDF p. 168 of `tmp/sources/hartshorne-1977-algebraic-geometry.md`) applied to the finite normalization would make $\OO_{X,Q}\to\OO_{\widetilde X,\widetilde Q}$ an isomorphism and $Q$ regular, so $\mm_Q$ maps into $\mm_{\widetilde Q}^2$ and the pullback has positive degree again; while a degree zero line bundle is $\OO_X(D_0)$ for a divisor $D_0$ supported in $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ by IV.1.9(c), whose pullback has degree zero. The card's step `s6-regular` transcribes it in the card's own notation, with $Q$ written $P$ and $\OO_X(Q-P_0)$ the identification $\mcl\cong\OO_X(Z-P_0)$ that step `s6` derives. Four steps the answer leaves to the reader are supplied there and marked as supplied: that $\mm_{\widetilde Q}/\mm_{\widetilde Q}^2$ is one dimensional, because $\OO_{\widetilde X,\widetilde Q}$ is an integrally closed noetherian local domain of dimension one and hence regular by Theorem I.6.2A; that the normalization is finite, which is Exercise II.3.8; that the map of local rings is injective, from the normalization inducing an isomorphism of function fields; and that the pullback of a Cartier divisor supported in $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has degree zero, from $\nu$ being an isomorphism over $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$. The answer uses neither $p_a=1$ nor the locally complete intersection hypothesis, so it places the point of every degree zero class in $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ on any integral projective curve; it also does not use the length-one computation, which is why the card keeps both.

**Not Vakil, 2026-11-17: the regular-curve source stays the regular case.** Vakil 19.9, printed pp. 555--556, is a regular projective geometrically integral curve; (19.9.2) supplies the existence half of `s6` and nothing about singular points. The card's published-solution remark now says so, and its sentence that the regularity step "is the card's" is replaced accordingly.

**What the card's step `s6` says now, 2026-11-17.** The existence half is unchanged in substance: a divisor $D$ supported in $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ with $\mcl\cong\OO_X(D)$ by IV.1.9(c), $E=D+P_0$, $\ell(E)=1$ by step `s3`, a section $s$, the effective Cartier divisor $Z$ with the sequence $0\to\OO_X\to\mcl(E)\to\OO_Z(E)\to0$, and $\length(Z)=\deg E=1$ by IV.1.9(a), so $Z$ is supported at a single closed point $P$ and $\mcl\cong\OO_X(Z-P_0)$. The regularity of $P$ is step `s6-regular`, which is KReiser's argument, and the conclusion $\mcl(E)\cong\OO_X(P)$, $\mcl\cong\OO_X(P-P_0)=\Phi(P)$ follows it. The card's earlier length-one route is kept as one sentence of the same step and marked as forcing the same conclusion: $\OO_{X,P}/(a)\cong k$ makes $(a)$ maximal, hence equal to $\mm_P$, hence principal, and $P$ regular by I.6.2A. That route is one line and needs no normalization, so the two-case argument is written out because it is the published one; a reader who takes the shorter route still has the published argument beside it. Nothing is weakened: no hypothesis is added to the statement, and steps `s1`--`s5`, step `s7` and every earlier audit event stand unchanged.

## 2026-11-17: V.4.9 is closed on Gruson–Peskine's five-squares criterion, the card's contraction step gains the two justifications it was missing, and its Egbert sentence is corrected

**The obligation and where it stood, 2026-11-17.** Two records of this file held `P-AGH549MINGENUS` (V.4.9) open. The entry "Chapter V: exercises whose Egbert entry is a citation, a stub or an unfinished computation" lists V.4.9 among the cards owing "a complete published solution of each", and its Impact paragraph describes the card's own derivation as "contraction to $X_2$ plus an effectivity/nef argument in the $X_r$ case". The Chapter V batch record's per-card list says of V.4.9 that "neither printed bound is proved … Open." Both stand as written; this record changes their verdict on V.4.9 and edits neither.

**The lower bound is the necessity of Theorem 2.5 and the attainment is Proposition 2.1, 2026-11-17.** L. Gruson and C. Peskine, *Genre des courbes de l'espace projectif. II*, Ann. Sci. École Norm. Sup. (4) **15** (1982), 401--418, Numdam `ASENS_1982_4_15_3_401_0`, read in the text version `tmp/sources/gruson-peskine-1982-genre-courbes-espace-projectif-ii.md`. For a class $C$ on a smooth cubic surface they set $d=-C\cdot K_S$, $r=d-\max\{C\cdot E:E^2=E\cdot K_S=-1\}$, $F_d(r)=1+\frac12\bigl((r-1)d-\frac34r^2\bigr)$, and the genus of a smooth connected member is $g=F_d(r)-\frac12\sum_2^6\alpha_i^2$ in the coordinates of an adequate basis. Proposition 2.1, statement on printed p. 407, is the existence half: for $0\le r\le 2d/3$ and $g$ with $F_d(r-1)<g\le F_d(r)$ such that $8(F_d(r)-g)$ is a sum of squares of five integers of one parity and of absolute value at most $r$, there is a nonsingular connected curve of degree $d$ and genus $g$ on $S$ with $r(\OO_S(C))=r$. Theorem 2.5, statement on printed p. 409, is the converse, so between them they decide every $(d,g)$ with $g\le1+d(d-3)/6$, except the printed triples $(d,g,r)=(9,1,2)$, $(23,22,4)$, $(27,28,4)$. The five integers are read as nonnegative, as the proof of 2.1 requires: it takes $0\le\alpha_i\le r/2$ in the even case, where the five entries are $2\alpha_i$ and may vanish, and five odd $\beta_i$ with $\abs{\beta_i}\le r$ in the odd case.

**The case $r=2$ is the whole exercise, 2026-11-17.** $F_d(1)=5/8$, so $g>0$ has $r\ge2$; and for $g\le F_d(2)=(d-1)/2$ the criterion reads $8(F_d(2)-g)=4\bigl((d-1)-2g\bigr)$ as a sum of five squares from $\{0,4\}$, leaving $(d-1)-2g\in\{0,\dots,5\}$ and $g\in\{(d-1)/2-j/2\}$. For even $d$ only $j=1,3,5$ give an integer, so the genera at most $(d-1)/2$ are $(d-2)/2$, $(d-4)/2$, $(d-6)/2$, and Proposition 2.1 attains the least with $(2,2,2,2,2)$; for odd $d$ only $j=0,2,4$ do, giving $(d-1)/2$, $(d-3)/2$, $(d-5)/2$, the last attained with $(2,2,0,0,0)$. A genus above $F_d(2)$ is at least $\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor+1$, which already exceeds both printed bounds. So the lower bound and the attainment in the printed ranges follow from the two statements with no further machinery — no Lemma 2.6, no asymptotics of $\Phi_d$, no table — and of the three exceptional triples only $(9,1,2)$ lies inside a window, at the odd degree 9 the printed range excludes. This derivation is arithmetic on the two statements and is the card's own; the statements are the article's.

**The table on printed p. 411 is the independent check, 2026-11-17.** It is headed "Tableau des lacunes pour $d\le41$" and its rows run over $d=10,\dots,41$ only, so no degree at most 9 has a lacuna and $g=1$ is realised at $d=8$, which is the even range's endpoint. In each of the 32 rows the column headed $F_d(2)$ reads $\{1,\dots,(d-6)/2-1\}$ for even $d$ and $\{1,\dots,(d-5)/2-1\}$ for odd $d$ — the printed $\{1,2,3\}$ at $d=13$, $[1,4]$ at $d=15$, $[1,17]$ at $d=41$ — which is exactly the initial segment the $r=2$ computation forbids and nothing else, and which leaves the bound itself as the least genus. The table therefore confirms both printed bounds and the attainment for $10\le d\le41$, and its omission of the exceptional triple $(9,1,2)$ is consistent: at $d=9$ the pair $(9,1)$ is realised and $8(F_d(2)-g)=24$ is not a sum of five even squares at most 4 each, which is what makes it the first exception.

**Bourbaki 592 supplies the framework and is not a solution of the exercise, 2026-11-17.** R. Hartshorne, *Genre des courbes algébriques dans l'espace projectif [d'après L. Gruson et C. Peskine]*, Séminaire Bourbaki exposé 592, Astérisque **92--93** (1982), 301--313, Numdam `SB_1981-1982__24__301_0`, text version `tmp/sources/hartshorne-1982-genre-courbes-bourbaki-592.md`. Theorem 0.1, printed pp. 301--302, classifies the pairs $(d,g)$ of a curve in $\PP^3$ by the surface containing it; Theorem 0.2, printed p. 302, produces a curve of degree $d$ and genus $g$ on a smooth cubic surface only for $g>\frac{1}{\sqrt3}d^{3/2}-d+1$, which at $d=10$ is $9.26$ against $(d-6)/2=2$ and stays above $(d-6)/2$ for every larger $d$; Theorem 0.3, printed p. 302, is the quartique case. So none of the three says anything about the bottom of the genus range, where this exercise's minimum sits, and none of them closes V.4.9. What the exposition does supply is the framework: its §1 quotes the class criterion of Hartshorne V.4.12 and Ex. V.4.8 in the form $a\ge b_1+b_2+b_3$, $b_1\ge\cdots\ge b_6\ge0$ imply an irreducible nonsingular member, except for $(n;n,0,\dots,0)$ with $n>1$, which is what the card's contraction-pullback step and its two equality classes use; and Remark 2, closing §1 after the proof of 0.2, states that Gruson and Peskine give there a converse of its Lemma 1.1 "qui leur permet de calculer, pour un degré donné, la liste des lacunes" — that converse is 2.5. Only Theorems 0.1--0.3 were anchored to printed pp. 301--302 by the supplied brief; §1 and the Remarques carry no page in this record, and Remark 2 is at the end of §1 and not on p. 302, a claim the first version of the card's remark made and its second commit of this date removed.

**The characteristic question is one-sided, 2026-11-17.** Bourbaki's §5 records that Gruson and Peskine "ont supposé que le corps de base $k$ était de caractéristique $0$, pour pouvoir utiliser le théorème de Bertini", and gives a characteristic-free substitute as Theorem 5.1. The lower bound of V.4.9 is the necessity direction of 2.5 and uses no Bertini — it is the structure of invertible sheaves on the cubic surface — so it holds in every characteristic. The attainment uses Bertini, hence rests on Theorem 5.1 in characteristic $p$, and neither source read here carries that out in the exercise's setting. Hartshorne's own convention is an algebraically closed field with no characteristic fixed, so the exercise asks for both. The card now says this, and the characteristic-$p$ attainment is stated on it as not settled.

**Two justifications were missing from the contraction step, 2026-11-17.** Step `repeat-contraction-until-x2-or-positive` stated its conclusion for $(-1)$-curves and then argued about lines, and its induction that every line of the surface reached has nonnegative intersection with $D$ was missing the step that carries it down. Both are supplied in the card now. First, on $X_r$ a curve $L$ with $L^2=-1$ has $L\cdot K_{X_r}=-1$ exactly when $p_a(L)=0$, by adjunction, so the $(-1)$-curves are precisely the curves of anticanonical degree 1 and square $-1$, which is what a line on $X_r$ is; on $X_6$ these are the 27 lines of the book's Theorem 4.9. Second, if $\sigma:X_r\to X_{r-1}$ contracts $E$ and $F'$ is a line of $X_{r-1}$ with strict transform $F=\sigma^*F'-mE$, then $m=0$, because $-K_{X_r}=\sigma^*(-K_{X_{r-1}})-E$ makes $F\cdot(-K_{X_r})=1-m\le0$ for an effective curve, which ampleness of $-K_{X_r}$ forbids; so every line of $X_{r-1}$ is the strict transform of a line of $X_r$ and the induction is exhaustive. Nothing else in the proof changed. The rest of the arithmetic was re-read and stands: $g-\frac{d-6}{2}=4+\frac{c(c-6)}{2}+(c-2)s+p$ for even $d$ and $g-\frac{d-5}{2}=\frac72+\frac{c(c-6)}{2}+(c-2)s+p$ for odd $d$, with the $c=0$ case $g=(b_1-1)(b_2-1)\ge s-3$, and the two equality families $2(h-e_1)+(s-2)(h-e_2)$ and $h+(h-e_1)+(s-1)(h-e_2)$.

**Egbert's V.4.9 is a draft, and the card said otherwise until this date, 2026-11-17.** The card's remark read "A. Egbert, *Solutions to Hartshorne's Algebraic Geometry* (2013), …, V.4.9, printed p. 290 (the minimum genus of a curve in a given class on the cubic surface)", which is a description of the problem and not of the entry. The entry is an abandoned computation printed with its working notes: "move $2.5\sum b_i$ here", "schwarz won't help", "let's evict $\frac12$", "hmm move $2.5b_i$ here", then four "case"s among which "if $\sum b_i<0$, $a=0$, then we are done", and no statement of either bound. Its "Existence" paragraph does reach for the right tool — it quotes "all positive integers $n<3k^2-2k+3$ is the sum of five squares … with $\abs{x_i}\le k$ (see ex 4.7)", which is Bourbaki's Proposition 2.1 — but it then fixes $b_6^2=3$ and applies the lemma with $k=a$, which does not keep the degree $d=3a-\sum b_i$ it is meant to realise. The card now records this.

**The papercut: neither article is in the Zotero export, 2026-11-17.** `vocabularies/references.yaml` carries no entry for Gruson–Peskine II or for Bourbaki 592, and that file is generated from Zotero by `tools/sync_bibliography.py` and is not to be edited. CITE-1 asks for a Pandoc citation with a Better BibTeX key, so these two attributions are prose with author, title, venue, series, volume, year, printed pages and the text-version path, which is the form the sibling "Published solution" remarks of `SRC-TEXT-HART77` already use.
